There's an old tradition of the law that, if evidence has been obtained either through threat or inducement, it is not available to the prosecution.
That was within the context that the Canadian Courts were not capable of having a conviction. My question to the Minister is: what inducements or what threats were made to Hambleton for him to make such a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INFORMATION AVAILABLE TO ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I was discussing the law that was applicable. I was not discussing the facts. The hon. gentleman can apply the law to the facts as he wishes.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Minister of Justice. There is a law with respect to the admissibility of statements, but I am asking the Minister, within the context that he told the press that there would not be a prosecution in a courtroom of Canada as a result of obtaining this subsequent evidence because it would not be admissible either through threat or inducement, was there any threat or any inducement that would prevent his Department from instigating a prosecution against a spy who gave away the secrets of our country to the Russians.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think 1 see the Hon. Member's problem. He is drawing a conclusion which I did not draw. 1 did not say there could not be a prosecution subsequently in this case. I said if one were to consider whether there were to be a prosecution, one would have to look at these principles of evidence.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. It concerns the interesting speech of the Prime Minister to a Liberal gathering on the weekend. The Prime Minister, at a $150-a-plate Liberal dinner, said that economic recovery was at hand. Unemployment at this point in the year is up 55 per cent over last year. On Friday, Statistics Canada indicated that the 15-month trend of a decline in the economy was no reason to believe that improvement was just around the corner. Considering that we are now losing jobs at the rate of 1,700 per day, does the
Government have access to information which has eluded the rest of us, or is this simply what Liberals pay $150 a plate to hear?
[ Translation]

Madam Speaker, perhaps my hon. colleague would care to look at the statement I made in the House on October 27 of this year, when I said that the Government was expecting to see economic recovery in the last quarter of this year and during 1983. 1 also said on that occasion, as the Hon. Member is well aware, that we expected high levels of unemployment to continue into next year, unfortunately, despite the fact that the economy would be showing a positive growth rate. Those are the predictions I made in the House at the end of October. They are the same predictions we are using today in projecting economic growth for the coming months.

The Minister carefully avoided dealing with what the Prime Minister had to say. No one in his right mind, at this point in December, 1982, would assert that recovery is at hand. We have the worst level of unemployment since the last depression and every indication is that the situation is getting worse, not better.

subsubtopic: BOWATER LAY-OFFS-REQUEST THAT COMPANY BE INVESTIGATED
speechtext:
I would like to ask the
Minister a question which is directly relevant to the job situation now in Canada. Last week my colleague, the Hon. Member for Churchill, raised a question concerning the layoffs by Bowater in Corner Brook, of some 700 employees. At that time the Hon. Member for Churchill pointed out that this company, in spite of significant profits recently, was shutting down. This plant is putting hundreds of Canadian workers out into the street. The Minister indicated that he would be prepared to look at this situation.
Today it was learned that the assertion made last week was absolutely true, that Bowater has paid $33 million in dividends in the last two years, based on a profit of $44 million which was earned here in Canada, mostly in Newfoundland. Is the Liberal Government prepared to investigate this foreign-owned company which has taken profits earned in Canada out of Canada, put Canadian workers out of a job, and transferred its profits back to Great Britain? Will the Minister investigate this?

subsubtopic: BOWATER LAY-OFFS-REQUEST THAT COMPANY BE INVESTIGATED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in order to help the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party see the situation in more exact terms regarding the economy generally, I would like to remind him that housing
December 6, 1982

starts in November, for instance, on a seasonally adjusted basis were at approximately 135,000 units. In October they were only at 107,000 units. Housing starts were up 30,000 units in a single month. Therefore, there are indicators that there is a turnaround, and there are some positive elements talcing place in the economy.
As far as the point raised by the Hon. Member is concerned,
1 indicated to his colleague last week that 1 was taking his suggestion seriously and I would examine whether there were any particular steps which should be pursued following his representations. I thank the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party for the information he has provided today, and I will certainly make sure that this is pursued further.

Madam Speaker, as 1 have said in another context, the people of Canada are getting just a little tired of the Government of Canada studying situations. They want, just for a change, some action by the Government.
In this particular context, we are losing hundreds of jobs, as I have said, at the rate of 1,700 per day. In the last few days it was Bowater, a foreign owned firm in Newfoundland; a couple of weeks before that it was the Iron Ore Company of Canada in Schefferville, a company which earned millions of dollars in profits in this country but was busy transferring those profits abroad.
Given our concern about jobs, instead of emasculating FIRA is the Government of Canada prepared to do what other industrialized countries have done with equivalent agencies, that is to say, improve the powers of FIRA so it would have the authority to ensure that profits earned by foreign firms in Canada are reinvested in Canada to produce Canadian jobs?

Madam Speaker, it is typical of the New Democratic Party to suggest action before they themselves have thought about it. That is not the style of this Government. We want to act, but after getting the proper facts, not on phony assertions which may be made right and left. We are going to get the facts and decide whether action is required, and we will act decisively if action is required and justified in the circumstances.
As far as FIRA is concerned, the previous Minister of Finance and the Government have indicated that we are improving the efficiency of the operation of FIRA.
What does "efficiency" mean?

We intend to go on doing so. The steps have already been announced in last June's budget, they have been

subsubtopic: CASE OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR-APPLICATION OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice and relates to the Hambleton spy matter, but more particularly with respect to why spies in Canada are apparently not prosecutable. The Minister will understand that we in Canada, because of the ineptitude of the Government, have become the laughingstock of the world with respect to the prosecution of spies, people who are taking information and selling it to foreign countries. The Minister has indicated that the Official Secrets Act is too broad, and he has indicated that the Treu case and The Toronto Sun case are examples of that. I would point out that those cases involved domestic disclosure of classified information, whereas in the Hambleton matter we are talking about the sending of information to our enemies.
Does the Minister feel that spies can be prosecuted under the Official Secrets Act? If not, where are the amendments to the Official Secrets Act, and would he please table in this House the legal opinion of his predecessor as to why the prosecution in the Hambleton affair could not proceed?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mark MacGuigan (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: CASE OF CANADIAN PROFESSOR-APPLICATION OF OFFICIAL SECRETS ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my hon. friend is asking for a great deal of legal advice in one question. The law applicable here is the Official Secrets Act, as he said. This is an act of this Parliament. We endeavour to give this meaning and application in every case in which it is brought forward to us. I have spoken of the fact that there are some deficiencies in

December 6, 1982

that legislation, and I hope to bring forward amendments to remedy them, but in the meantime we will certainly in good faith attempt to apply the Act in every case where the facts warrant. When facts come before us we judge them on the basis of that Act and the traditional interpretation of that Act, and of course on the weight of the facts themselves. That is exactly the kind of decision that my predecessor made with respect to the Hambleton case.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I only have to refer to the Prime Minister's statement at his press conference last week in which he indicated that the Department of Justice is always doing that, that is to say, always advising against the prosecution of spies in our country.

TIMING OF DECISION TO PROSECUTE IN GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 have a supplementary question for the Solicitor General. Over the weekend he posed the incredible and novel proposition that somehow the Security Force in Canada was using reverse psychology in telling Mr. Hambleton to beware of a hostile reception in the United Kingdom.
First, when was the Government actually aware that the United Kingdom was going to proceed with the prosecution of Mr. Hambleton? Second, what was the deal between Canada and the United Kingdom with respect to proceeding in the United Kingdom as opposed to proceeding in Canada in the prosecution of the alleged spy, Hugh Hambleton?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: TIMING OF DECISION TO PROSECUTE IN GREAT BRITAIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, as to the headlines, which I also read, speculating about reverse psychology, I can assure the Hon. Member that I said no such thing. In none of the articles that I read was such a position attributed to me. It is speculation, and it just hangs there for what it is worth. I have not said that the Security Service informed him that he would be prosecuted if he went to Great Britain. He was informed that he might receive a hostile reception.
I would remind Hon. Members that the British interviewed him for a long time after he went back to Great Britain. It may well be that the prosecutorial decision was made on the basis of what he said after he arrived in Great Britain. We were not informed, and it was not indicated to the Security Service that the hostile reception would be prosecution. It was simply indicated that he might receive a hostile reception.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CONSIDER ESTABLISHING EMERGENCY FUND
speechtext: Madam Speaker, may I put a question to the Minister of Finance. In his responses to questions in this House in the last number of weeks, he has often been forced to say that there is nothing the Government can do in the short run, to combat lay-offs in all parts of Canada. Perhaps there is a solution that the minister ought to consider. Municipalities across Canada, such as Kamloops and Salmon Arm, have capital works projects ready to go, in the amount of $18 million each. If the Minister is interested in job creation and in stimulating the economy from one end of Canada to the other, would he give some consideration to establishing a special public works emergency fund so that muncipalities across Canada could get these road projects, sewer and water projects and parks projects, that are now waiting for financial support, off the ground?

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER CONSIDER ESTABLISHING EMERGENCY FUND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will consider any suggestions put forward by anyone in this House. I will give all suggestions very serious consideration.

December 6, 1982
Oral Questions
As a general statement, however, 1 should like to point out that it would be very wrong for provincial or municipal Governments to sit on their hands and hope that the federal Government is going to dish out hundreds of millions of dollars to them. Municipal Governments and provincial Governments, like the federal Government, have the power to borrow. If there are projects which are worth-while for the community, I encourage them to exercise their responsibilities as elected officials, to go ahead with the projects, to go to the market and borrow money like the federal Government is borrowing, and to do something that is required in the community. They should not wait for the federal Government to finance every action which is taking place in the country.
As I indicated, the federal Government set aside over $1 billion in addition to the previous amounts set aside for direct job creation last October. This is a significant amount of money which we are putting aside for all kinds of job-creation programs across the country. 1 hope municipal Governments, like others, will do their share in this regard, and try to use this period of recession to stimulate activity, proceed with projects which they themselves can finance on their own, and not just wait for grants from the federal Government. This being said, 1 take the statements of the Hon. Member as a representation. As I said, I will consider it together with numerous other representations which have been made by other Members.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance as well. It concerns the announcement made by his colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, on his behalf last week, of the imposition of a very significant new tax burden on northern residents, a burden which will result in an increase of between $2,000 to $3,000 per year for the average worker in the North who is employed in the mining and resource sector industries.
Could the Minister tell the House why he chose this particular time to make this imposition on northerners, having regard to the fact that they are already hit hard and that economic circumstances multiply themselves several times by the time they are experienced in the North? Why is it that he imposed this tax at this time?

Madam Speaker, I should like to tell the Hon. Member three things. First, the announcement was not made by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on my behalf. I made it myself, and I associated that Minister and the Minister of State for Mines with this particular announcement.
Second, the tax will not generate the figures to which the Hon. Member referred of $2,000 or $3,000 per individual.
Third, there is no tax. The remission order is being continued in 1983 and, as a matter of fact, it is being extended to workers who were not covered by the remission order in 1982. They will benefit from an exemption in 1983 which was not available to them in 1982.
The taxation of benefits will only start in 1984. It will start on a very gradual basis. The taxation of benefits will grow 25 per cent a year. It will start with only 25 per cent of the taxable benefits being eligible for taxation. The figures to which the Hon. Member referred are quite small and I would like him to bear that in mind when he considers the steps that have been taken, which I think are quite fair to the people of the North who were benefiting from the particular remission order.

This is a display of a strange twist of logic. The Minister says that it is a tax which was always on the books but had never been paid and that simply because it has to be paid now it is not a new tax. I must have attended a fairy-tale session last week when I sat in on the press conference, including stations of the CBC northern service, when the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, announced a new tax.
In fact it is not a serious imposition when it is figured out on a monthly basis, as the Minister did but, when the monthly figures are multiplied by 12, it is an imposition of between $2,000 and $3,000 on average taxpayers or average northern workers. There are no ifs, ands or buts about it.

Madam Speaker, did the Minister of Finance take into consideration that the average home owners in the North pay between $200 to $300 in some instances for utilities to heat their homes, that they pay $4 for a gallon of gasoline, and that freight costs often multiply essential consumer commodities by four times? Is there any equity and fairness in his tax system at all? Why was logic not considered, that changes to the tax Act would have been a much better compromise to replace the remission order?

Madam Speaker, I remind my hon. colleague that the average northerner never had access to this particular benefit. It was limited to a very restricted number of people who happened to work in the North for large corporations or certain Governments. That was the limit of the benefits. They were not available to the average northern citizen or resident. Indeed we have very carefully taken into account the serious recession which the industries in the North are knowing at the present time by not imposing the taxation of those benefits in 1983, and by starting the taxation of them on only a gradual basis in 1984. It will take four years after 1984 before they become fully taxable.
In addition, we have put specific ceilings on benefits such as housing allowance, for instance, so that there would not be

excessive taxation of these people. 1 invite my hon. friend to examine more fairly the proposal or the plan which was announced, and he will come to the conclusion that he should not be talking about the kinds of figures he indicated.

appropriate institutions. It does this on a continuing basis by advising on and reviewing the priorities of the Library, its developments and its ongoing activities. It is also an important channel for making known the services of the Library in the Provinces and for soliciting suggestions for making its services more responsive to the needs of its users.
In the period under review, the Board met three times. In October, 1980, the meeting was held in Saskatoon and at a public session the Library's programs were summarized, questions were entertained and briefs were received. In November, 1981 the National Library Advisory Board met with the Advisory Board on Scientific and Technical Information to discuss Telidon and its application to library and information services. As a result of this meeting, the Board recommended that the National Library act as a clearinghouse of information on the applications of videotex and teletext to library services.
During the two fiscal years under review, the Board furthered the development of a decentralized network to facilitate the exchange of bibliographic data and the sharing of library resources. This recommendation was first set out in the "Future of the National Library of Canada", presented to the Secretary of State in 1979, after extensive consultation across Canada and with the support of the National Library Advisory Board which assisted with the establishment of priorities. In particular, the Board established committees to investigate in depth and make recommendations on some of the issues posed by the application of the combined technologies of computers and telecommunications to the evolution of a bibliographic network as well as those which need examination for the sharing of data and library resources. The progress made in these areas has resulted in the formation of the Bibliographic Common Interest Group, co-ordinated by the National Library, as part of the iNet (intelligent network) trial mounted by the Computer Communications Group of the TransCanada Telephone System. Six libraries with autonomous computer systems are able to interconnect to exchange bibliographic data and to facilitate document delivery. The Board also received recommendations concerning electronic publishing, the legal aspects of network development and the unauthorized use of copies of databases and requested that these issues be investigated.
In the same period, the Board made formal recommendations to the Secretary of State on the establishment of national library services for the visually and physically handicapped. It also actively supported the Library's submission to the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped which recommended that the Library act as co-ordinator of Canadian library services. As a result of the proposal, endorsed by the Special Committee in its report "Obstacles", the National Library received the resources to set up a program in 1982/83.

He said: Madam Speaker, this Bill is being presented to implement one of the elements of the six and five program announced in the June 28 budget.
Shame!
This program is a cornerstone of the Government's program of economic stabilization and renewal.
Not a cornerstone, a millstone.

I might remind the House that the purpose of the six and five program is two-fold. First, it is intended to set a clear example of federal leadership so that we can deal effectively with the problems of inflation, high interest rates and unemployment and to make our economy more productive. The second objective of the program is to provide funds to be reallocated to job creation.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-124, the Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act passed by Parliament last summer, was the first in a series of measures to reduce inflationary income expectations. The Bill restricted wage increases of employees in the public sector to 6 and 5 per cent, for a period of two years. Another measure applied the 6 and 5 program to the inflationary component of indexing of family allowances, old age security pensions, public service pensions and personal income tax. Thus, the purpose of Bill C-133 is to apply the 6 and 5 program to public sector pensions. The bill is not a pension policy but should be seen as part of a comprehensive response to the economic problems facing Canada today. As I said before, it is one of the many economic measures that were contained in last June's budget.
In that budget, people who have been employed in the federal public sector and who therefore have more assured incomes and relatively more job security than most other Canadians were asked to accept less protection from inflation temporarily so that inflation could be reduced and the Government could free up needed financial resources for job creation in the private sector.
Bill C-133 does not single out federal Public Service pensioners as the cause of inflation any more than any other group of Canadians. Rather, the Government chose the public sector
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
as a vehicle to project an unmistakable signal to all of the participants in the Canadian economy that we have to have lower income and price increases if we are to deal satisfactorily with problems of inflation, the problems related to it of high interest rates as well as the problems of unemployment.
Nobody believes that. [Translation]

Mr. Speaker, the general goal of the program is to encourage the private sector to follow the example set by the Federal Government and its share to reduce inflationary demands on the economy. In Bill C-133, cost-of-living adjustments paid under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act are capped at 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. These restrictions will apply to all individuals receiving retirement benefits as a result of employment in the federal public service.

Without this legislation, public service pensions would be increased by 11.5 per cent in January of 1983. This percentage reflects the full cost of living adjustment prescribed by the present law. That adjustment of 11.5 per cent would arise out of the relative increase in inflation in the 12-month period ending in September, 1982 over the average increase in the previous 12 months.
The restraint program is designed to alter inflationary expectations. It seeks to counteract the expectations of inflationary increases and the resulting future inflation which comes from assuming that price performance in the past will turn out to be the case for days yet to come.
Since Bill C-133 received first reading there certainly has been a fair amount of public discussion surrounding it, principally by those who oppose it. The debate has also produced a great deal of confusion and factual error over the nature of the present indexation arrangements. I would like to deal briefly with some of those more common misconceptions at this time.
Many of those who oppose the limitation on increases in Public Service pension indexation argue that public servants have fully paid for their indexation through their contribution of 1 per cent of salary, together with the matching direct contribution by the Government as employer, towards the cost of this benefit. This is not the case. Approximately 90 per cent of the indexation benefits paid to Public Service retirees are currently charged directly to the Consolidated Revenue Fund of the federal Government.
Fine way to make a case.
The Consolidated Revenue Fund is made up of moneys raised from the taxpayers of Canada generally.
That is right-you bet.

Only the balance of the indexing benefit, that is approximately 10 per cent of those payments, comes directly from the supplementary retirement benefits account. This is

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
the separate account set up to receive employees and employer contributions to provide for pension indexation.
To explain why this is so, I would remind Hon. Members that the present law provides what amounts to full indexation for inflation to all Public Service pensioners and their survivors. But an indexation program was first introduced only in 1970 and a large number of such pensioners retired before that date. Those who retired before 1970 made no contribution for indexing, and the majority of those retired in the years since 1970 have contributed only a small portion of the over-all costs of the benefits being paid.
Those critics of Bill C-133 who are aware of all this say yes, but if the supplementary retirement benefits account was combined with the basic pension accounts, there would be sufficient funds to support full indexation. Again, this is not the case. Looking at the program as a whole, if funds were taken from the basic accounts to support full indexing, shortages would arise in these accounts so that the basic pensions would no longer be properly funded.
Some of those who have commented on Bill C-133 have referred to an alleged $14 billion surplus in the public service superannuation account.
They are crazy.
I am informed that no such surplus exists.
That is right.

The $14 billion presumably refers to the balance in that account as of the last fiscal year end, that is, March 31, 1982. The balance at this time is in fact $15.5 billion. However, the important thing to note is that this money represents the amount which, together with future interest earnings, is needed to pay the accrued basic superannuation benefits-the basic pension-to all existing Public Service pensioners and their survivors, as well as the benefits which have been earned to date by current employees.
Other arguments have been made to the effect that the Government has broken a contractual agreement with its pensioners and has also violated an agreement that unilateral changes would not be made in the public service pension plan without prior consultation with employee representatives. While 1 regret that prior discussions did not take place before the June budget on this matter, 1 can only say that this measure was proposed as part of the over-all restraint program announced in that budget, and that it is not normal practice to reveal measures, so announced, in advance.
The capping of indexing for inflation is a temporary measure for two years which is, of course, quite different from any permanent changes which might be proposed for the plan and which would be discussed in advance.
With respect to the alleged contractual nature of pension arrangements, as Hon. Members are aware, there is no formal contract which parallels the written wage contracts existing between the Government, as an employer, and its employees. While 1 gather there was consultation with employee representatives on the question of providing full indexing for
inflation of Public Service pensions prior to that program being implemented, it in fact came about through a Bill introduced by the Government and approved by Parliament in 1973. Therefore, it would be more realistic to view such pension arrangements as being long-term but, at the same time, flexible and involving the employer and generations of employees, where changes can be made in the relevant legislation to reflect varying economic circumstances.
This was, in fact, what happened in 1973 when Parliament adopted the policy of full indexing of Public Service pensions and took the additional step of applying that policy retroactively to many persons who had paid little or even no extra contributions at all. Also, another modification to reflect economic circumstances was made as part of the Anti-Inflation Board program when Parliament put a cap on Public Service indexing to limit it to an increase of $2,400 for 1976.
Notwithstanding these comments, however, and due in large measure to the representations of several members of our caucus supporting the Government, the Government has given additional consideration to how six and five should apply to the Public Service pension arrangements. The Government recognizes that there are retirees who have made some contributions towards the cost of indexation and that moneys are set aside for this purpose in the supplementary retirement benefits account. The Government has accordingly given further consideration to whether the capping measure should apply both to that portion of the benefits paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. As a result, it has concluded that indeed the capping should not apply to both of these portions.
Therefore, I propose to move, at an appropriate later stage in the debate on Bill C-133, an amendment which would be based on the principle that the six and five cap would apply only to that portion of the indexing which would be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund-that is, from general tax revenues-but not to the indexing which would be charged against employees' credits in the supplementary retirement benefits account-that is, coming from direct contributions by employees and by the employer specifically for indexing.
Such an amendment would be in keeping with the Government's over-all approach on the application of the restraint measures to federal allowances and pensions. That is to say, as the House knows, the Government has proposed that the programs financed out of general tax revenues, the Family Allowance and Old Age Security, would have temporary limits placed on their increases in indexing for two years. However, the Canada Pension Plan, for which direct contributions are made by employees and employers, has not been included in the six and five restraint program.
The effect of the amendment will be to limit the increase in Public Service pensions to 6.5 per cent in 1983 and 5.5 per cent in 1984. The funds available for reallocation to job creation after adjusting for the proposed change are estimated to be $60 million in 1983 and $105 million in 1984.
December 6, 1982

1 want to stress that the Government remains committed to the principle that retired Canadians have protection against the effects of inflation. That is why we are proposing that over the next two years indexing for inflation for recipients of the Old Age Security and the Public Service pension will continue up to the limits to be set for the restraint program. The six and five program does not reduce any inflation protection which has been paid to date. What is proposed is a limit on the amounts for increases in indexing payable from general revenues during the restraint period.
As I said earlier, Canada Pension Plan benefits remain fully indexed, as do the income security benefits of those drawing the Guaranteed Income Supplement so that a measure of full inflation protection will remain on a portion of the incomes of many retirees, including recipients of Public Service pensions. More important, though, is the effect of the six and five program on breaking inflationary expectations. As the consumer price index, interest rates generally and mortgage rates come down, any real income losses from the cap on increases in indexing will disappear.
I know that the introduction of this Bill and the public discussions surrounding it have raised many questions about the state of the superannuation and indexing accounts. These include questions on the funding and financing of the program, the philosophy behind the use of the funds in the accounts and whether the various accounts should be combined, just to name a few of the issues or questions. However, I regard these as long-term issues and I believe these must be addressed in the context of the debate which will take place over the coming months about the direction and form of our national pension system, both public and private, once the green paper on national pension reform is released later this month.
Let me assure everyone that there will be full opportunity for consultation before any changes are decided upon and any proposals made to Parliament concerning the superannuation plans of federal Public Service employees. In passing, I want to recall the work done on these issues by the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee in a previous Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians should be very happy about the successful results so far of the 6 and 5 program and the promising signs of further success in the near future. We are getting closer to the 6 and 5 era, which is the purpose of the first stage of this important program.

A review of retail prices since the June 28 launching of the program shows inflation moderating. On an annual basis, inflation in October was an even 10 per cent, the lowest rate since May, 1980. On a monthly basis, inflation in October was 0.6 per cent.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, considering the 0.5 per cent recorded in July, August and September, we can certainly say that inflation is stabilizing at the levels we have set. If we continue this trend,
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
it will also help to stabilize the real income of Canadians, including retired Canadians.

To conclude, let me repeat that this Bill is part of a broad policy package intended to steer us toward lower inflation and renewed economic growth. Therefore, I urge all Members to support this Bill and its early adoption.

Mr. Speaker, we have just heard an extraordinary speech by the Minister. Just a few moments ago in one of the last passages of his discourse to the House, the Minister said there would be full consultation before any changes would be made in the superannuation program affecting the public servant. It is interesting to note that that promise about full consultation was made some time ago. It is precisely that promise which the serving public servant and the superannuates say was broken.
I do not know why anyone in the federal Public Service, anyone who represents federal public servants or anyone who is interested in the question of equity and good conscience in terms of this matter should be prepared to accept that representation by the Minister. He read carefully from a prepared text. I do not know why he should expect that when we had similar undertakings from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the former President of the Treasury Board with respect to the same kind of consultation-no changes regarding inflation as an eroding power on superannuates' income.
Earlier in his speech the Minister said, and none of us is quite sure what he meant, that this amendment would limit increases in 1983 and 1984 respectively to 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent. I believe that is what he said. What he is saying to this House is that with 0.5 per cent, "I can buy you". That is what he is saying to all the people he is today asking to support his program.
Instead of having a six and five program, apparently it is now a 6.5 and 5.5 program. That is what he seems to be suggesting to the Members of this House. We will have to examine it in some detail, but that is what he said today.
I am going to deal with the problem that affects certain members of this House of Commons and a little later, I hope, a much larger number. If anyone who is interested in this program regards it as a great leap forward in equity, they had better think about it overnight. They will have some time to think about it before they leap and grab at this, clutch it and hold it close to their bosom as a salvation.
What this represents is not a great victory but a failure by Members of Parliament to persuade the Government. They did their best to attempt to succeed with respect to this, but it is a great failure.
The Minister was very careful not to tell this House what this Bill is. He set it in a broad framework. I will tell Members what it is. It is part of a vicious trilogy of legislation being dealt with in this House of Commons. We are not through dealing with it all; This is the third leg of the vicious trilogy of legislation.

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act {No. 2)
The first piece of legislation, which affects those who are not in a position to look after themselves, is Bill C-131 dealing with the recipients of Old Age Security. The Government decided that the senior citizens would be put into the trenches to be the cannon fodder in this fight against inflation.
The second thing they are saying is that mothers of young families, the young children themselves, are to be the second tier in the trenches behind the Old Age Security recipients under Bill C-132 dealing with Family Allowances and limitations thereto.
The third leg in the trilogy is the public servants. That is an interesting phrase. Let me tell you what that means in terms of who it affects, Mr. Speaker. Broadly speaking, it affects every serving public servant because the six and five program as applied in Bill C-124 has an effect thereafter on their best six years. It affects every retired public servant because the six and five program as applied in Bill C-124 has an effect thereafter on their best six years. It affects every retired public servant because the retired public servants are grateful for the support willingly given to their superannuation by those who are still working. It affects every serving and retired employee of every Crown agency and Crown corporation in the country. It affects the Members of this place, certainly, and Her Majesty's judges. More importantly than that, if affects every member of the Canadian Armed Forces, both serving and retired. It affects as well those who are serving and those who have served in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The group which is sometimes forgotten in all of this discussion about six and five is not just those who are still in the work force in the broad public sector and, therefore, have some clout in terms of future bargaining, but the wives, the widows and the children of those who are serving and those who have served. Those are the ones who are affected by this piece of legislation.
I am going to characterize this Bill, even with the amendment which we are going to have a chance to look at and the figures which are going to be produced later on, in this way: it is a mean, vicious, wretched, immoral act of this Government. That is how it ought to be characterized. Any Government which would put those who have retired into the trenches with respect to the battle against inflation and run them ahead of itself as the shield against inflation ought to be ashamed of itself.
I do not think the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) ought to count this as a red letter day in his ministerial life. This is his first major piece of legislation. Bill C-119 was his first piece of legislation and that was nothing of which one can be terribly proud. In fact, it has not yet even been scheduled at the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee. In any event, I do not believe the Minister should be proud that his first major piece of legislation is a Bill that breaches faith and an undertaking and defies a moral obligation. Whether this Government likes it or not, the funds with which we are dealing, never mind the statements which have been made,
every contribution which has ever been made over the last 50 years, is a contribution of funds which are impressed with a trust. If you or I, Mr. Speaker, tried to convert moneys impressed with a trust from one purpose to another, the Crown Attorney would be called in. Governments are no better than anyone else, even majority Governments. It is a breach of a moral obligation to the serving public servant as well as those who have served in the broad sense I have described, including the wives, the widows and the children.
This piece of legislation is unsupportable. The gall of this Government in this matter is breathtaking, to move in that direction and then to say, "But we will consult a little further now". What happened to the consultation before? Our Party is opposed to this Bill; make no mistake about that. This piece of legislation to cut indexing for serving and retired public servants so that their incomes in retirement will not reflect the cost of living is being proposed by the same Government which decided it would be a good thing one way or the other to index mortgages. It said that in the budget. The Lortie Commission dumped on it, but that proposal has not gone to sleep because the Economic Council of Canada has decided it would be a good thing to index mortgages for, supposedly, younger people buying homes, people still in the work force who can protect themselves. But with respect to that group of public servants who are said to be docile, quiet, who do not make much noise and are not very popular in the country, "We'll deal with them; we'll cut their indexing. We won't let that be reflected".
There is another side to this, Mr. Speaker. This same Government which is asking for a cap on indexing is exactly the same Government which looks after its friends. You must have read in the paper, as I have, about the generous golden handshake for the senior public servant, Michael Pitfield. It is marvellous what the Government has done for him with respect to his pension. It is allowing Michael Pitfield to leave the Public Service with a special deal which will allow him to contribute to his indexed Public Service pension at a certain rate so that when he has reached the period of life when he, too, can no longer bargain, he is going to be protected, even though he did not serve, even though he decided to leave voluntarily. It is generous, Mr. Speaker. This is what the Order in Council said, and I quote:
-to approve ... the continued participation of Mr. P. M. Pitfield under the Public Service Superannuation Act on the basis that he shall contribute 50 per cent of the contributions payable under the act until such time as he takes his pension, the other 50 per cent of the contributions to be paid by the Government-
1 should add, a "grateful" Government. The article continues:
-and ... to deem ... the salary of Mr. P. M. Pitfield to be at the 8th decile of the DM-3 level as amended from time to time until he takes his pension."
What is that level?

What is that level, my hon. friend asks. At his present rate of pay, it could easily total $100,000 by the time he is eligible for retirement at the age of 55 on June 18, 1992. There is still a Santa Claus, Mr. Speaker. And yet, for the least of the public servants, for the least of the
December 6, 1982

widows, for the least of the children of public servants, that Minister has the gall to stand up in the House and say: "We are going to do it for Pitfield, but we are not going to do it for you".
Well, Mr. Speaker, we do not intend to stand idly by and see that kind of thing happen. The Government might as well face up to that. Technically, Michael Pitfield could have worked for the Government for 20 years and be paid for 40 through his pension, at the level of a Deputy Minister. That is really generosity worth noting in this country. Yes, Virginia, there is a Santa Claus! Is there not someone over there who can blush at that? Cannot the former President of the Treasury Board, who has now gone to his glory in another portfolio, blush at that? Is there no one over there who does not see the injustice of it all? Is there anyone over there as my friend, the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) says, without a sense of shame? I hope there is. I hope there is someone over there with the guts to stand up against that kind of inequity for the least of those in the Public Service.
Does the Government need to renege on its contractual obligations, Mr. Speaker? I am going to read from a letter to the Editor of the Ottawa Citizen where that question was put. This is the answer:
The refusal to honour indexing commitments for public servants would reduce the government deficit by less then $60 million in the present fiscal year (based on an average contribution per pensioner of approximately $450 less income tax). That is a substantial sum, but placed against a budget deficit of $23 billion, it will not do much to reduce inflation.
What is really at stake is public trust and confidence in the government. While it may be politically opportune for the government to make public servants and public service pensioners "whipping boys" to divert attention from much more serious matters, the question is, who will be next? Will the government decide to default on other contract commitments?
In the conduct of affairs, whether they be public or private, the "broader principle" is that there must be rules for the game. Neither governments nor individuals should be allowed to change the rules to fit personal convenience. In that direction lies chaos and anarchy.
That is the reason the community is aroused about this matter, whether you are talking about old age pensions, mothers' allowance or this Bill in particular. It is a breach of trust, pure and simple, a breach of a moral obligation. That is why we oppose this Bill.
Members know the history of this legislation, Mr. Speaker. They know it has been some 50 years in development. They know it was Arnold Heeney who indicated clearly that there was an undertaking and obligation to serving public servants which ought to be met. When public servants of that day wanted to have pensions bargainable, the Government said no, that could be difficult. It could lead to all kinds of anomalies and problems. "Do not make it bargainable and we will make a deal with you; we will not change those things without consultation".
That is the history. The Government held to the bargain for a long period of time. In 1973 the Government finally took the 2 per cent cap off. I spoke for my Party in 1973 and said it was a good thing. Why? Because indexation does not put public
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
servants marching ahead of the economy; it keeps them up to date. It just keeps them in line. Why is it a good thing that we keep those people in line? For the same reasons that we keep recipients of the Canada Pension Plan in line-because we have a special obligation to those who have gone ahead. This Bill is a denial of that obligation. I read in 1974 the directive of the Treasury Board that said it was the policy of the Government to keep everyone in line to ensure that no one would lag behind. That was the reason for indexation. I read what the Prime Minister said in a letter to the National President of the Defence Employees' Association. This is what the Prime Minister said on October 12, 1977:
In our society, pensions provide a means of sharing risk so that we can retire in reasonable security and dignity, without fear of the future. Protecting pensions from inflation by indexing them to increases in the cost of living should be an integral part of our pension schemes.
It was, it is, and if this Bill fails, it will still be. He goes on:
Indexing does not give pensioners an increasingly larger claim on our economy's production-
Remember that, my friends in the Liberal Party; that is what your Prime Minister said. He continued:
-that is, more money to buy things they could not earlier afford. Rather indexing merely enables pensioners to maintain, roughly, their same standard of living.
I do not normally quote the Prime Minister, but it may be only the Prime Minister whose words will have some influence on those over in that party who can change the course of this legislation if they want to. The Prime Minister went on to say this:
Even a modest rate of inflation destroys, at a devastating rate, the buying power of people on fixed incomes. Pensioners are out of the workforce and cannot bargain or strike for larger incomes. They are not the cause of inflation; they are its victim. We have an obligation to help protect them.
That is what the Prime Minister of Canada said in 1977 when the problems facing pensioners then were not as serious as they are now. If that was the truth in 1977, why has it suddenly become the anti-truth in 1982? Why has the situation suddenly changed? When he said that, the need for protection was not as great and the disparity was not as great as it is now. Yet today, when we have all those problems, and with increasing uncertainty, suddenly the Liberal Party, the Liberal Government, changes course and puts all pensioners in the front line of the fight against inflation.
In 1981, the then President of the Treasury Board said it was the position of the Government that public servants would be protected from inflation. At the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates not too long ago he said, in answer to a question of mine, that it was not the intention of the Government to bring in legislation to deal in isolation and individually with Public Service pensions.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He is listening to you now.

But that it would be considered as part of an over-all program of pension reform. That is fair ball, but this is discriminatory. When you move a Minister from one portfolio to another, does it mean that what

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
was the truth before can become a lie today? 1 suggest not, and no one in the country will believe it.
You will never convince, Mr. Speaker, the serving public servant that the money we are talking about does not belong to him, that he did not contribute, that there is not a contract or an obligation, because the argument is irrefutable.
As best 1 can, I have given the history and this will be examined in committee if the Bill goes through. The Bill will never get to committee, of course, if some Members of the Liberal Party do their job.
1 am told the legislation would rob the average pensioner of about SI,200 over the next two years, would impoverish them and drastically lower their standard of living. Some people think that Public Service pensions and the pensions paid to widows are huge and that these people walk around with their pockets heavy with coinage from the pension to which they have contributed through an arrangement made by the Government. That is not so, Mr. Speaker. Former public sector workers and their survivors currently receive an average pension of only $6,900. That is better than nothing, but it is not a large pension. These are the people who will be affected by the Bill.
1 think that the public should know that the Senate of Canada maintains that a two-person family earning less than $11,030 in 1980 was said to live in abject poverty. The Government would like to weave a fantasy of wealthy public servants with both feet in the public trough. But that is not so, Mr. Speaker. Even if it were partially true, any Government would have to think twice before it attacked those who cannot protect themselves; but that is what the Government is doing through this Bill.
I want to speak to my friends in the House who have spoken out about this legislation, Mr. Speaker. The discussion first started in the warm days of July, 1982 when the breezes that flowed over the Ottawa River had a remarkable effect on some Members. The Ottawa Citizen of July 9, 1982 quoted the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) as follows:
I personally find it unacceptable that the government plans to limit pension indexation. The government is a trustee of the indexation fund but the money belongs to the pensioners.
No doubt the Hon. Member will be speaking in this debate and will develop what I think is a fairly reasonable theory about where payments can be made. If he speaks, he will condemn the President of the Treasury Board for the line of reasoning he has brought forward. I certainly expect him to enter this debate and to oppose the Bill.
Then the Hon. Member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle), who is in the House listening to the debate today, spoke on the matter when the proposal to limit indexation was included in one of the MacEachen budgets. The same Ottawa Citizen article reported him as saying:
-they should leave the pensions at full indexation. Eighty per cent of retired civil servants are not getting very big pensions and most are out of the workforce so they can't increase their incomes.
I agree with him; he is right. Some time during the course of this debate I want him to stand up and say this. When the time comes, I want him to put his vote where I believe his mouth is-that is, to oppose the Bill.
The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), who is my good friend, is also in the House today. That Ottawa Citizen article quoted him as saying:
I have not seen any evidence that the contributions paid to the supplementary fund are inadequate and that the fund is not solvent.
I want to take a good hard look at the government proposals.
I assume he has taken a good hard look, Mr. Speaker. I shared a platform with him at the RA Centre the other night when he made what I call a courageous speech, indicating that he opposed the Government's proposal to reduce indexation to six and five. 1 presume he will not be purchased or bought by 6.5 and 5.5.
Then there is the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates on which I have the honour to serve and which will deal with this Bill. According to that Ottawa Citizen article he said that the pension indexation fund:
-is similar to investing your money at a trust company. There is now $889 million in the indexation fund and it is paying a 14.9 per cent return on investments.
That is not bad, Mr. Speaker. He went on to say:
Suddenly one day the trust company phones up to announce that arbitrarily and unilaterally it will only pay six per cent because the customer is expected to set an example.
He was also at the public meeting at the RA Centre. He and I had the privilege of sharing the platform. At that time he gave us a trust company analogy in both official languages and he said he was going to stand against this measure. There was not a public servant of the some 800 in the hall who did not understand that and left the meeting with content in his heart that the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) was on his side.
At that great meeting at the RA Association there was also the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). He had been denied a pension. He said he was opposed to this, that he supported indexation, that this was not the Government's money but it belonged to public servants. He pointed to the audience of public servants and superannuates who agreed that it was their money and who cheered him to the rafters. They even tolerated him when he said that, on the other hand, he was a Liberal and would not want to vote against the Party. He gave the clear impression, however, that his heart was in the right place but that his vote might be in the wrong place. It was marvellous that night. There was an ecumenical euphoria in the hall when Liberal after Liberal stood up and said: "We are opposed. We will vote against it.". One said, "We do not want the Tories in office again; we don't want to risk it." I will help them out with suggestions about how we can get around that in a few minutes, Mr. Speaker.
I want to talk now about something that has worried me. I go to church from time to time and every now and again my minister warns me against backsliding. The Hon. Member for
December 6, 1982

Provencher (Mr. Epp) understands what I am coming to. I suspect the person who spiritually ministers to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier has warned him against backsliding from time to time as well. That is why 1 was shocked to read the headline in the Ottawa Citizen of November 25, 1982: "Grit MPs back off from revolt over PS pensions".
As 1 have said, as the Hon. Member for Provencher has said, as the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) has said, as the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) has said, as the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) has said and as the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has said, they could hardly believe what they read, in view of the courage that had been exhibited at the Recreation Centre in front of 800 public servants. The Member for Ottawa-Vanier said they were worried about bringing down the Government; that it was a matter of confidence in the Government if they voted against the Bill.
1 agree that it is a serious vote, given that the President of the Treasury Board characterized it as an absolutely essential part of the six and five program. I just do not believe the President of the Treasury Board when he says that it is essential, but that is his view. In any event, these Liberals have indicated that it would be a blow and that they were worried about bringing down the Government.
I will help them out because I believe the fate of the Bill does not lie with the New Democratic Party or with the Progressive Conservative Party. Its fate lies with the backbenchers of the Liberal Party. The question of retired public servants lies with those Members of the Liberal Party who are prepared to put their votes where their mouths are. There may be more. The rate of this Bill also lies with those who believe in simple justice and wonder whether it is right to deny a moral obligation which has stood the test of time, which has been backed by the Prime Minister and by former Presidents of the Treasury Board, and which has been relied upon by people who made their retirement plans on the basis of these things, those who are no longer in the work force. I want my friends opposite to remember that there are federal public servants in British Columbia, Alberta,.Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec and the Maritime Provinces. blow to the Government for sure, but it would be a blow to the Government worth sustaining. I put it to my friends that it would not bring down the Government. Mr. Speaker,
I noted with interest the comments of the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). In his closing remarks he stated that this was a breach of contract. He should realize that when the six and five program was brought in under Bill C-124, which his Party supported, it was also a breach of contract with many Canadians across the country. He and his Party supported it. In fact, his Leader stated that they had not gone far enough. Now the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) is starting to go a bit further.
It is a sad day for me that I have to rise in the House to speak on Bill C-133. It is difficult to discuss the Bill before the House of Commons because so much of the language which we need to describe the Bill is unparliamentary. For example, it removes pension protections for which public servants have already paid. What do we call a person who takes something that belongs to another person without that person's consent? This is what I want to ask. The Bill also provides a pension level less than that promised to public servants. What do we call it when a person sells something to another person and delivers much less than he promised?
Then there are the Conservatives. The Conservatives say they oppose this Bill. They say they oppose it in the same way they oppose the Bill to reduce indexing on Old Age Security. But what are the Conservatives going to do with that opposition? They are not going to do very much. Even last November 18, when the subject of Bill C-133 came up in the House, the Conservative House Leader asked the Government House Leader whether he would bring the Bill forward the following day so they could deal with it expeditiously.
There is also a word for a person who claims to oppose something but then does nothing to back it up. We cannot use any of those words in the House of Commons. If we cannot use the words describing what this Bill really does in Parliament, we can at least describe the effect it will have.
First and most important, this Bill will permanently reduce by 10 per cent the real incomes of over 150,000 retired federal public servants. Thousands more widows or retired public servants will see their incomes cut as well.
Once again, the Government has tried to say that this Bill will only affect people who can afford to be affected. The average pension of people retiring in 1982 is $8,100. The average pension of all retirees from the federal Public Service
is $6,900. The average pension going to widows of public servants is $3,200.
Let us put these figures into perspective. A couple living in one of Canada's largest cities requires an income of nearly $12,000 annually to keep above the poverty line. If inflation for 1983 and 1984 remains in the area of 10 per cent, which seems likely, people retiring this year will see their real pension income decreased in purchasing power by about $1,400. People receiving survivors' pensions will see their purchasing power drop by over $500. While this is happening, there are no guarantees about prices. What happens when housing costs and rents go up, energy and heating costs go up, food costs go up, medical costs go up, a factor very important to senior citizens?
Pensioners are not just facing a temporary loss of income. When our economy recovers and our workers return to their jobs, they may be able to catch up with some of the losses they have incurred. They may do this through productivity or bargaining. But pensioners will never catch up because they will never have that opportunity.
This Bill and Bill C-131 impose pension cutbacks which will reduce the incomes of retirees for the rest of their lives by making their pension base lower. That is a fact that must be understood.
One idea that must be put to rest in the House today is that the pensions attacked by Bill C-133 are some sort of Government charity. They are not. They are pensions which have been bought and paid for by working public servants.
Since 1924 public servants have had sums deducted from their wages to pay for retirement pensions. Like many employers in the private sector, the Government also makes contributions to the pension funds and interest on those funds is added. The difference is in the amount paid by public servants. Public servants pay a base rate of 6.5 per cent of their salaries into pension contributions, which include the Canada Pension Plan. Over and above that amount, and this must be understood, public servants pay a further 1 per cent of their salaries into an indexing fund to cover the costs of indexed pensions. In fact, public servants pay one of the highest pension contribution rates of any employer-sponsored pension plan in Canada. The Government is also aware that there is enough money in the pension funds to pay the pensions of retired public servants, even though the Government has paid a very low rate of return on the money it has held for pension purposes.
Public servants have chosen to pay a larger portion of their incomes into pension plans than other people, and for a very good reason. They know that pension plan contributions are a form of deferred income. They are putting off a portion of their income today for their future needs. Public servants chose to put off a larger than usual portion of their incomes in order to guarantee themselves a secure retirement, protected from the ravages of inflation. Throughout their working lives public servants paid a portion of their pay cheque to give themselves a safe future. On the basis of that indexed pension, which they had paid for, many public servants have taken an early retirement.

That secure future, paid for during their working lives, is now being threatened by this Bill, which will reduce their standard of living by 10 per cent. In essence, we know that pensions are nothing more than a way of putting off earnings until retirement. The Government, through this Bill, is, in effect, confiscating a part of those previously earned wages. For working public servants, wage controls will affect their present and their future wages. Retired public servants, through this Bill, are actually having their wages reduced retroactively. The pension indexing which is being stolen from these retired public servants has been acknowledged as a vital part of their pensions. Let me quote one important commentator on this subject as follows:
-Put simply, people must be protected in their retirement years. The Canadian Government has pledged that they will be better protected in the future than they are now-[DOT]
Pensions which are not protected against inflation naturally tend to dwindle over the years. People who thought they had purchased protection for the rest of their lives find that they have more serious financial problems the older they become. The unfairness of that situation, particularly when the savings pool to which they have contributed may have been reaping inflationary interest premiums, is not tolerable in a nation which believes in social justice-
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said that at the 1981 National Pension Conference. For the President of the Treasury Board to bring in this Bill now on behalf of the Government of Canada is a disgrace and a shame.
However, the then President of the Treasury Board made similar comments to those of the Prime Minister last year concerning public service pensions. He agreed that our pensions were indeed simply deferred wages and said:
The federal Government remains dedicated to the principle that public servants' pensions are to be protected from inflation.
I see the former President of the Treasury Board is sitting in his place and laughing. He will not be standing up with some of his backbenchers who have indicated that they may vote against this Bill. No doubt they will be properly told to get back in line.
The action being taken by the Government is so morally wrong that it has even forbidden companies in the private sector to do the same thing. Pension plans, registered under the Canada Income Tax Act, are prohibited by law from reducing either benefits or any right to benefits of a supplementary pension. What is illegally and morally wrong for insurance companies is now before the House as Government policy.
When collective bargaining was being introduced to the federal public sector many years ago, the Government approached the associations which existed at that time. The Government proposed to exclude superannuation from collective bargaining. In return, the Government said there would be unilateral changes in the program. That was a gentleman's agreement. It is now pretty clear just how much a gentleman's agreement with a Liberal Government is worth. It is something like the iron-clad guarantee made by the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources when we were dealing
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2) with the Alaska pipeline. I imagine there are some retired public servants who are now wondering just how much the word of any Liberal Government is worth.
Less than 6 per cent.

I think they must also take into consideration the fact that when they elect these members, it is the policies of the Liberal Party and of the Conservative Party for which they are voting, not the individual. It is evident that the individual cannot carry the load for the electorate and cannot entice the Government to carry out programs for the protection of the people.
Just a couple of weeks ago, the Public Service unions in this community held a public meeting for retired public servants. Nearly 1,000 people came. Many were turned away, as was mentioned by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) during his speech. However, before that audience of 1,000 people, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) and the Hon. Member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) promised that they would fight the Bill and vote against it. Those were pretty tough fighting words.

That is how the meeting dispersed that night. In fact, when I returned to the House I found that there was no vote being held in the House.
Cowardly behaviour.

Mr. Speaker, no doubt some will find it strange that I should be speaking this afternoon; first, that I should have chosen to speak and, second, that the Government should be allowing me to speak this afternoon on this Bill in view of the remarks that I have made publicly and which I will be repeating this afternoon.
The reason I have chosen to speak is that I have heard so much rhetoric from Hon. Members of the Opposition in the last several days on Bill C-131 and C-132 that I felt that for my own constituents, at least public servants and retired public servants in my riding, it would be a good thing for me to put my position on the record in totality, so that there is no misunderstanding about the position I have taken on this Bill.
I have just listened to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker), which remarks do not surprise me. It is same socialist line we have been hearing in the last several days. I will allow only one thing: it is consistent with what I expected to hear from him. In fact, he only said one thing that surprised me. He said he found it difficult to discuss the Bill. I would have thought he would find it very easy to discuss the Bill. Certainly I will not have any difficulty in discussing the Bill. However, I will particularly address my remarks this afternoon toward the Tory Party, because it is the hypocrisy which I have heard from that Party in the last several days which makes me angry enough to want to speak this afternoon.
First, I have publicly said that I do not like Bill C-133, and I repeat it. It is simple. I do not like it simply because we are reducing the expectations of retirees from the Public Service. We are cutting down the amount that they were expecting to receive in 1983 and 1984. That is a fact and no one can deny it. However, it should be abundantly apparent that if we succeed in reducing the rate of inflation in 1983 to 6 per cent, the amount they will receive next year, 6 per cent, will compensate them for the increase in the cost of living.
Which, of course, brings us to the Government's efforts to reduce inflation and to do it across the board. I must ask myself, first of all, whether it is fair to apply these reductions to the superannuation payments of public servants. Certainly I have publicly said that I believe that public servants have, with their own money, purchased something. I will come to the definition of "something" in a minute. They believe that they have purchased full indexing of their pensions. However, with what did they pay for full indexing? Those who retired previous to the imposition of the charge for indexation paid nothing whatsoever. Those who have retired since, those who retired before 1975, have paid one-half per cent. Those who have retired since 1975 have paid 1 per cent.
Quite apparently, even with a person who has recently retired in the last year and has contributed to indexing since the 1975 change to 1 per cent, or the one-half per cent prior to that, the amount of that contribution is certainly inadequate to cover the amount of indexation for all the years ahead. Thus one could argue that if the amount is inadequate maybe the Government should have approached it in a different fashion, that it should have increased the levy on public servants. That is one approach that one can take.
I have also argued that the Government, and I hope this will happen fairly soon, should put together the amount that is in the fund to cover indexation with the amount that is in the original fund to cover pensions, and that these two together should be enough to cover indexing in future years. It should be abundantly apparent that even the amount that is presently in the fund to cover indexation is more than enough if we can reduce the rate of inflation to a low level of, say, 3 per cent, 4 per cent, or 5 per cent.
I did indicate at the meeting which was held on Monday evening, November 22, at the Recreation Centre in Ottawa, that I did not like Bill C-133. At the same meeting I was asked the direct question: "Will you vote against Bill C-133?" I said: "No, 1 will not". I want to explain that in full right here and now.
First of all, I was elected as a Liberal to support Government policy.
Even if you do not agree with it.
Government policy at the present time is the full program of six and five.

Hear, hear!

1 support that in its entirety. The Tories, I had thought, also supported it in its entirety. I must admit that when six and five was originally introduced 1 did not think all the way down the line. 1 did not think down to the level of the old age pensions and to the level of Family Allowances.
You did not think at all.

I am on the record already as stating that, in the case of Family Allowances, we should start economizing. In fact, I have even suggested freezing Family Allowances entirely, not even increasing them by 6 per cent. I suggested that we put some sort of a freeze on the basic old age pension and that we index only those receiving the GIS, indexing the total, of course, of the GIS and the OAS together. The reason I suggested this is that I believe that when the Government is short of funds, when there is an obvious need to direct our moneys to those most in need, we should make every effort possible to redirect our funding to those who are likely to suffer the most from the present high rates of inflation.
1 find the arguments that are based on universality frankly hypocritical. I admit that that is a plank of my Party and I have no hesitation in supporting the principle of universality. I also point out that, as long as we have the OAS universal and the GIS revenue-tested, as long as we have Family Allowances universal and the Child Tax Credit means-tested, and so on and so forth, we only go as universal in our programs as we can afford.
In principle one can support universality, but I have bluntly asked the Members of the Socialist Party on several occasions, if there is a shortage of funds to whom do we give the money? Do we share it among everybody? Do we share it among my constituents who are well above average in income, or do we try to direct that funding at those who need it most?
1 find it quite incredible that the Members who have spoken in the last few days on behalf of the Tory Party should so work on the emotions of people in this country. I have heard all kinds of things said by the Tory Party but we know for a fact that if they ever were to form a Government in this country they would crucify the social programs that presently exist. If you look at the total spending on social programs, the only way they can achieve their end result of a balanced budget is either to increase taxation, or decrease social programs, and in either case the poor will have to pay. So let us discard this rhetoric that we hear from the Tory Party.
How are you going to vote? What is wrong with the amendment? You could vote on that one.

We can talk as much as we want about reducing spending, but another thing is important. Will no Member of the Tory Party who supported the principle of six and five, stand up and admit that if all programs continue to be fully indexed, then we will carry into 1983 the rate of inflation which exists in 1982?

That is nonsense.

Since the objective is to cut the rate of inflation in 1983, then we have to anticipate what the rate is likely to be and reduce the carry-forward to that level. That is why, much as I detest Bill C-133-1 say so publicly and I have said so before-and much as I do not like the fact that the pensioner is not going to receive as much as he or she anticipated he or she would receive, if we are going to stick with our principle of six and five, which is to reduce inflation by not carrying it forward into the following year, then we have to do it right across the board.
I suggest to the retirees, the public servants who are now on pension, that the amount that they are going to contribute is no more or no less than the amount that everyone in this country is being asked to contribute. I say to retirees that their contribution, difficult though it may be, is going to help us to achieve the objective of a 6 per cent inflation rate next year. I feel that if we make an exception for the retiree, we have to make an exception for the old age pensioner. Typical Liberal.
