He offered some suggestions with respect to negotiations that might help restore some of the money to the public servants' trust fund with respect to the indexation part of that fund. Would the Hon. Member take kindly to the hoist of the Bill for six months to allow him to use his good offices to make that negotiation and bring some fairness to it, as suggested by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker)?

Mr. Speaker, if it was that simple, I would give a simple answer and the simple answer would be yes. However, the Hon. Member knows, as everyone in this House knows, that if this Bill is not passed by January 1, an 11 per cent increase goes into effect.
Eleven and a half.

Approximately 11 per cent, if the Hon. Member wants to be precise. The point is that unless this Bill is passed before January 1, the increase according to the present legislation will go into effect at that time. 1 will give him my word on one thing. I do not give up on an issue. Even if this Bill goes through, I am not giving up. 1 want to see a change made in this legislation so that we will not again be in the position where we have to go through this particular exercise.

Mr. Speaker, as 1 rise to address Bill C-133, I want to refer an old biblical adage to my
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
friends to the left, paraphrased somewhat. It goes something like this: Let he without sin cast the first stone.
I wonder how many times my friends on the left have wondered in their hearts and minds about the craftiness of the resolution which brought down the 1979 Government. 1 wonder how many times they have felt that they are reaping the whirlwind because they, with the majority of Canadians, are having to suffer the frustrations and the desperations of this Government.
It is the second time in a very short period that I rise, with other Members in this House, to address a pensions Bill. The short period of time is made shorter because of closure by this Government on Bill C-131. That is an act to limit the time for discussion and debate, an act to prevent the public from realizing the length and extent to which this Government is going to pin the problems of Government on the pensioner. The pensioner should not be the one to bear responsibility for the over-expending of this Government or the inflation which has struck us. In our wildest moments, as I said in respect to Bill C-131, we did not think that the pensioner would be in the front line of the restraint attack, the six and five attack. But that is what has happened and our Party is deadly opposed to Bill C-133, as we were with respect to Bill C-131.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), in the last minutes of his comments this afternoon, proposed to make an amendment. I suppose, true to the tradition of that Party, that amendment will be drafted more to bring his players into line than by what is in the best interests of pensioners. It will be a further variation of the six and five working together.
The Minister went on to say he would have to wait for the green paper before introducing equity and justice. We are told that the Government's green paper on pensions will be tabled within this next two weeks. That paper should have been the meaningful reform legislation upon which Acts such as this might be based, amended or related thereto, instead of bringing forward Bills C-131, C-132 and C-133, one after the other, to put legislation in place so that the reform paper will have no meaningful effect on pension reform.
How can a Government claim to be serious about pension reform when such a Government deals with pensioners as callously as this one does? How can a Government be serious about pension reform when it is prepared to destroy one of the bulwarks of any strong pension plan-the protection of pensions against the ravages of inflation? How can a Government point an accusing finger at the private sector for offering little more as protection against inflation when that Government is moving in the same direction? Finally, how can any Government hope to maintain credibility, trust and faith with its Public Service when it unilaterally goes back on its word, a signed agreement, in an exercise of political huckstering? And how else, Mr. Speaker, could one describe the Bill which was

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
presented this afternoon other than as an exercise in political huckstering?
Bill C-133 proposes to limit increases in Public Service pensions to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984, regardless of the inflation rate in either of those two years. This is done to save the Government an estimated $100 million over these two years. We on this side have grown to respect the sum of $100 million, unlike the big spenders sitting on the Government benches. However, we have to respect something else as well, the fact that some items of expenditure have greater priority than others. But how can one justify cutting Public Service pensions by $100 million when the waste, extravagance and mismanagement of our economy continues unabated? Anyone can pick up a newspaper at any time and read a tale of squander and waste. One can read where hundreds of millions of dollars are being spent in foreign shipyards because Canada lacks a shipbuilding policy. One can read where thousands of jobs are being lost because we lack a Canadian content agreement with respect to Japanese imports. One can read where another oil rig has left this country for the United States because of this Government's National Energy Program. One can read of a 70 per cent increase in the travel expenses of Ministers this year over last year, while they talk in terms of a six and five program. Against a background like this, Mr. Speaker, cutting a Public Service pensioner's cheque is not restraint; it is just simply being mean and misguided.
Last week a bright young fellow decided all Members of Parliament needed copies of all news releases which might be related to the six and five program. More than that, he decided that Members of Parliament needed that material indexed, prepared on high quality paper and enclosed in binders emblazoned with the "six and five" logo. This binder sums up better than any words possibly could the utter hypocrisy of both the six and five program and the Government's approach to the most serious depression we have faced since the 1930s. If restraint is to have any meaning, the Government must distinguish between governing in the best interest of all Canadians and governing in the best interest of the Liberal Party.
It is all right for me or for any other Member of Parliament to illustrate the 1,001 ways in which the $100 million could be saved other than by cutting Public Service pensions. But when we talk in terms of $100 milion, we tend to forget the real meaning of this Bill, the real meaning for those who will be affected by it. As of last month there were 90,000 former public servants receiving pensions. In addition, there were another 32,500 persons receiving survivor benefits. One reads about fat cat public servants and those huge, fully-indexed pensions which they are going to receive, and Michael Pitfield might just be in that category.
It might interest Hon. Members on both sides of the House to note that the average pension being received is $6,900. This, Mr. Speaker, is the "fat cat" which the Government wants to rein in or limit to six and five deindexing by way of Bill C-l 33. The Government says: "Oh well, the impact of the six and five program is not nearly as great as one would imagine". First of all, when your pension income is $6,900, every dollar counts.
Second, we are not talking about a meaningless amount of money which will be lost to those pensioners. Assuming inflation next year will be 11.5 per cent, and 10.5 per cent in 1984, the average pensioner will lose $1,409 over those two years, and the average survivor will have lost $557 from their "fat cat" meagre pensions. Once again, when we consider the average 1982 starting ground is $6,900, a loss of this order is anything but meaningless or "not so great".
The second reason for my opposition to this Bill is the very significant hardship being inflicted on individual pensioners. But there is a third point I want to make as well. We in the opposition are often critical of the Government's non-stop printing presses. Day after day, night after night, those presses are turning out what the Government calls information briefs or brochures. Some of us would prefer to call them propaganda brochures. One such product was the pamphlet prepared to let public servants know about their pension plan. Another was a much larger publication issued after the last National Pensions Conference. The first publication stated clearly:
All pensions are adjusted annually to cover cost of living increases.
That does not say, Mr. Speaker, adjusted to cover "some" increases; it says Public Service pensions are adjusted to cover cost of living increases. My mathematics may not be perfect, but 1 fail to see how a 6 per cent increase will cover 10 per cent inflation.
The National Pensions Conference held here in Ottawa in 1981, which I was pleased to attend, provided a forum for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to adopt a holier-than-thou attitude with respect to the private sector. I have to wonder if he is not wincing just a bit, trying to square this Bill C-l33, and Bill C-l31 with what he said at that conference. Put simply, he said people must be protected in their retirement years:
The Canadian Government has pledged that they will be better protected in the future than they are now.
Once again, perhaps a Government Member could explain how 6 per cent is better than 10 per cent. Or is it simply that a pledge is only a pledge when it suits the political fortunes of a Government bankrupt of ideas? Where is the fulfilment of trust when pensioners are being deprived of something they paid for? However, Mr. Speaker, our Prime Minister could not leave well enough alone. He had to go on to say:
Pensions which are not protected against inflation naturally tend to dwindle over the years.
I certainly do not argue with that statement of fact, Mr. Speaker. Nor do 1 argue with his conclusion:
The unfairness of that situation is not tolerable in a nation which believes in social justice.
Where is the social justice in Bill C-l 33 or Bill C-l 31 ? Does social justice take a back seat to the re-election hopes of the Liberal Party, which we heard about at length from the previous speaker? This Bill in no way, shape or form lives up to the Prime Minister's remarks at that conference, nor does it offer a legitimate reason why it should supersede what he said. As 1 have already pointed out, the $100 million saved could
December 6, 1982

have been and still can be saved elsewhere, but this Bill hurts those who cannot afford to be hurt in difficult or even in good economic times. I have shown that these phrases, uttered in the sanctimonious tones of many Government speakers at that pension conference, fly in the face of the obvious.
There is a final point which needs to be emphasized. The pensioners in question believed and still believe that they have a formal agreement with the federal Government on the question of indexing pensions. In return for paying 1 per cent of their salary into a supplementary retirement benefits account, public servants were to receive full indexation of their pensions. That, in essence, is what the Government stated it would do. Even more importantly, that is the spirit of the agreement and that is what public servants had been told to expect. To announce 12 years after the fact that the fine print allows the Government to weasel out of the agreement is a breach of faith and political opportunism at its worst. For three nights running the Prime Minister spoke to the nation about trust, confidence and belief in our political leaders. Who would ever trust a Government which would attack pensioners while leaving the JetStar engines idling while the Government waits for the next six and five binge?
I am appalled at the persistence of this Government in bringing this Bill forward. In 1979 a Conservative Government found over $500 million worth of fat to be cut without too much difficulty. The same could be done today if there was an effort put into that task. That money is five times the amount being saved by this legislation, yet the Government refuses to cut waste because it is easier to ram a Bill through this House by closure and enforced voting than it is to pore over departmental budgets and estimates. Well, if the Government has lost the will to control its own spending, call an election so that the Canadian people can determine where expenditure cuts can be made and decide whether the Government will have the will and determination to get spending under control.
While I am unalterably opposed to this Bill, Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago, as has been mentioned earlier today, several Government Members were just as equally opposed to that legislation. Now they feel the winds of non-confidence blowing in their faces and we hear an about-face and a very different story today than that told on an earlier occasion. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it will be a sad day for Canada indeed if Government Members opposite vote for opportunism, selfpreservation and self-protection rather than for responsible government, good government and the people they represent in Parliament. The Just Society of 1968 is most certainly dead, thanks to today's Liberal Party of Canada. Will they not just take six months more to reconsider their position?
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (N. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe it is important that Members for the various ridings concerned should make a contribution to the debate on Bill C-133 which is about to affect the indexation of Federal Public Service pensions. Mr. Speaker, I listened to the previous speakers and I also heard what the Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) had to say. I believe that in some parts of his speech he was right, while in others he was wrong. In any case, I am not going to try and analyze all the speeches made in the debate on Bill C-133. I think, in fact I am certain, that the Members opposite are electioneering on this subject. I also think that my friends in the New Democratic Party at least during the last election campaign totally ignored Section 32 of the Public Service Employment Act which precludes political activity by certain public servants. 1 am sure that to them, Section 32 applies only to Liberals and Progressive Conservatives. But quite honestly, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I, too, have had grave reservations and have given careful consideration to the implications of Bill C-133. I can honestly say that I am opposed to Bill C-133 in its present form. The reasons, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
Speaker, are simple. There is a matter of equity involved here, and if there was a mistake on the part of the Government that drafted the Act or the regulations or on the part of the bureaucrats who drafted this legislation when indexation was approved in 1970, we should certainly not try to correct the initial blunder by perpetrating a second one. Since we are on the subject of indexation of Public Service pensions, I think we should have had studies made, as suggested in 1976 when a report was tabled in the House concerning the entire question of Public Service pensions. However, it was not done, Mr. Speaker. The question came up again in 1978, when it was suggested that the procedure for indexing Public Service pensions should be changed not abolished altogether by linking indexation directly to the interest generated by the funds provided by employees, interest that could be redistributed to Public Service pensioners according to a given scale. The point was, Mr. Speaker, that in the case of galloping inflation, the interest generated would have been higher and the resulting funds would have been redistributed from year to year to retired public servants and would also have provided a basic scale for indexing wages. That would have been eminently logical, Mr. Speaker. We would not have been obliged to take this corrective action which 1 would qualify as grossly unfair via-a-vis this group in society which is no longer on the labour market.
Obviously, when legislation is introduced, there are exceptions for which provision must be made, and I think that the officials who prepared this legislation should and could have made an exception for retired public servants. Mr. Speaker, blunders are made. The other day, I noticed that a senior official who was Deputy Minister at Health and Welfare was transferred to Paris for a year, on the same salary he was getting before, while during that time his position was to remain vacant. The position in Paris calls for a salary that is $20,000 less than what the official was earning before. So he is getting the same pay he would be getting if he had stayed here in Canada, which is certainly a lot more than 6 and 5, Mr. Speaker and there are many other examples. In fact, the newspapers are full of them. So I hope these are not the same senior officials who drafted the 6 and 5 measures that apply to retired public servants, because we know what goes on in the upper echelons of the public service, Mr. Speaker. No one who has an important job is going to be affected by 6 and 5. They just change the category and the salary with it, and the 6 per cent will apply, as they say, over and above, so I think there is something here that we as legislators should do, but unfortunately, the system has not reached that stage yet.
When 1 see the Progressive Conservatives making modest attack on the system, and I said just now they were doing some electioneering, including my good friend from Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) who is not above adding an extra quaver to his voice to sound more convincing, I think the people listening should remember that when the Progressive Conservatives formed the Government in 1980, they said without hesitation that they were going to eliminate 55,000 public
servants. I do not want to indulge in electioneering, and 1 just want to-
IMr. Baker (Nepean-Carleton): That is no excuse!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (N. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
. . . 60,000, I apologize, I forgot 5,000. In any case, I do not want to do any electioneering, and 1 just want to defend the rights of the majority of my constituents who are public servants and retired public servants. I agree with the 6 and 5 program as a general government policy, and 1 congratulate the Government for having adopted this measure, but I also think that this bill should allow for exceptions, and Mr. Speaker, retired public servants are an exception. Where pensions are concerned, there is a big different between 6 per cent of $4,000 and 6 per cent of $30,000, because someone who is drawing a pension of $30,000 will get nearly $2,000 that is easy to figure out while 6 per cent of $4,000 is only $240. People on low incomes need every cent to make ends meet, while to someone who is getting a pension of $30,000, whether he gets an extra $2,000 or $1,800 does not make such difference, it is not vital, so that is why I am saying that this bill is unfair, because if we look at the principle underlying indexation, the whole point was to maintain the purchasing power of pensions so that retired public servants would continue to have access to the same market basket and the same services, and this is the principle the Government committed itself to. Mr. Speaker, this was said in this very House in 1978 by one of our colleagues, who unfortunately is no longer with us today, and who has served this country well, and I am referring to Bob Andras, an exceptional President of the Treasury Board, who wanted to change the system in 1978, and who unfortunately was unable to have this plan implemented. Mr. Speaker, we are forcing retired Canadians to submit to the 6 and 5 restrictions, while in most provinces-I am not referring to the Federal Government here, although I may later on-public utilities including gas, hydro and telephone services, all of which are essential services that no one can do without, let alone pensioners, are increasing at a stupendous rate every year. Take hydro, for instance. We have a surplus of electric power, but nevertheless, prices are still increasing at an astonishing rate in la belle province, although it is against all the principles of political economics, and the same applies to natural gas.
So why are we saddling our pensioners with this reduction in indexation? No one is going to get rich with a cost-of-living indexation, especially-but this is of course hypothetical-if we expect that in one or two years, indexing may be 7 or 8 or 9 per cent. If we were sure that indexation would go down, why not maintain cost-of-living indexation for the 85 per cent, that is, the vast majority of retired public servants who are getting not more than $4,000 or $6,000?
Mr. Speaker, I feel that these people have served their country well as public servants, and this includes the Armed Forces, the RCMP, and all those who have served their
December 6, 1982

country in the course of duty and when they were in a position to do so. 1 remember when 1 was growing up in the Ottawa-Hull area, that the Public Service had trouble recruiting employees. Mr. Speaker, that was because the pay was not good. Today, pay levels may be somewhat higher than they are in the private sector, but the fact remains that to get people the pay has to be good. If it is not, they will not come. Maybe we have gone to the other extreme, and perhaps a review would be in order. In fact, a study was made in 1978 or 1976.
There is a mass of data, and when senior officials talk about the subject, they reel off a whole series of figures which do not mean a thing to the average person. No matter how many speeches are made and no matter how many reasons are given, retired public servants will never understand, and they certainly have no reason to, why the Government is taking away what they paid for. That is what is happening. Never mind the figures, never mind that this is going to mean a savings of $50 million and that if we do not cap indexation it will mean an increase of $100 million. We all know how governments conduct their finances. They make budgets and they always have budget deficits. Why? Because there are contingencies, of course, but there are other things that also happen to a budget. The individual person, the retired public servant, however, was first asked to pay 1 per cent extra to cover indexation, and this point was made over and over again. Now all of a sudden they are saying: Listen, drop everything, the country is almost bankrupt and now you have to help us get it out of this mess. Well, I do not think that is the way things work. They do not see it that way, and I think they are right. 1 hope that during the debate it will be possible to make some changes-and I see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray)-to put as it were a more humane face on this question by making a special exception for retired public servants. Once more, we are in favor of 6 and 5, and personally, I would have said more about this question, because to the people, 6 and 5 means a reduction. A lot of speeches have been made and of lot of figures have been produced, but we forget to tell people that what was involved was a salary increase that was being capped at 6 and 5 per cent. We get people writing us who think it is a reduction. Some people say: If you do not vote against the bill, we will not vote for you in the next election. We always have voted for you but will not this time. But if they vote against the Liberals for introducing this legislation, they will vote against me in any case. When all is said and done, I think they are doing a bit of innocent blackmail, because they are good people. However, I am not doing this for political reasons and 1 am not trying to do the Public Service Alliance a favour. In fact, I have had it up to here with the PSAC. So 1 am not particularly keen on doing them a favour, I am doing this for the pensioners, because I realized that we were really hurting a sector of the population that is particularly vulnerable because it is no longer part of the labour market.
My contribution to this debate has been to the point and will, I think, be understood by everyone, even if 1 did not quote any figures. 1 was very reluctant to parade vast numbers of
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
statistics in order to impress or depress people with all the data we are able to produce. In any case I am sure that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray), with his natural intelligence, his sensitivity to the plight of the autoworkers in his constituency, his broad political experience, his great wisdom and his understanding of the human condition, will realize that perhaps it would be advisable to introduce amendments that will go somewhat further than the bill he introduced this afternoon.
Mr. Speaker, this was my humble contribution on the debate on Bill C-133, a bill which I hope will be amended for the benefit of retired public servants who have served their country well and continue to do so.

We voted against-

Let me try again. Bill C-l24 provided a small cut in the pay of Members of Parliament. The New Democratic Party opposed that Bill. That is the Bill we voted in favour of. It had nothing to do with the capping of indexation. Indexation capping is contained in Bill C-l31 and in Bill C-133, depending upon which pension is involved. But to try to say continually that because somebody voted for or against Bill C-l24 means that they vote for or against Bill C-133 is carrying things a little far.
After the budget was brought down, in the debates on the budget I raised the question on July 15 and again on August 2 that we were going to have to look at legislation, presumably in the fall, if we were going to carry out what the budget had indicated we would. 1 am particularly interested in pensions of servicemen and retired servicemen.
There are not too many Members in the Chamber who have a close interest in the Canadian Forces superannuation account or the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act as it applies to the Canadian Forces superannuation account. I have a great deal of concern about this matter partly because it is so complicated. When the Hon. Member for Winnipeg is not here, there is hardly anyone who can give you a logical explanation as to why the Government keeps putting money from one account into another. It seems these accounts are overflowing with money, but in fact there is no money there. 1 feel that a contract has been broken with the servicemen who paid their contributions faithfully. They now find they will not get the pension they expected.
It is difficult to understand the attitude of some of our friends on the benches opposite. They are well known. I believe the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton referred to them this afternoon. First, there is the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) who finds it unacceptable that the Government plans to limit pension indexation. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) said that the pension indexation fund "is similar to investing your money in a trust company" which then decides not to pay out on the agreed terms. Any trust company doing that would have its charter removed. The Hon. Member for Hull, who has just finished speaking, said that they should leave the pensions at full indexation. speechtext:
Whatever the Hon. Member for Hull does, he is not too specific about it. However, we will watch him with a great deal of interest when the vote comes. Then we have the vocal Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans). He said:
I have not seen any evidence that the contributions paid to the supplementary fund are inadequate and that the fund is not solvent.
I look at the funds quite often, and I have a great deal of difficulty finding that they are not solvent. 1 have tried to find out.
The last Member whom I shall refer to is the Hon. Member for Gatineau. He said:
I wonder if we can legislate on this matter since the money belongs to the pensioners.
What worries me is that a group of Liberal Members of Parliament can get together before 800 voters out there. These Members say something outside of the Chamber but say something quite different inside. We are witnessing that today, and it is not a nice thing to see, quite frankly. Members opposite go out and try to buy votes. They hope nobody will notice what they said. Then they come in here and hope that nobody will notice how they vote. One is opposite to the other, and it is embarrassing.
We have the prime example set by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He sent out his famous telegram saying that he indeed was very aware of all of this and that he had noted the concern about indexation of Government pensions, that is should be maintained.
The Prime Minister philosophizes in a letter in which he wrote:
In our society, pensions provide a means of sharing risk so that we can retire in reasonable security and dignity, without fear of the future.
It is sickening for the Prime Minister to write that and have it sent to pensioners. They depend upon Members of Parliament to look after their interests. It is a joke when we hear that things are ironclad agreements. An ironclad agreement is a joke because it means that you do not intend to keep the agreement. The Prime Minister of the country put the pensioners at ease. He said the Government had no intention of removing indexation from pensions, but here we have a Bill that is going to do exactly that. The sad part is that this is the time when pensioners need indexation the most. I will have a few more words to say about that in a minute or so.
I just wanted to point out that five Members of Parliament and the Prime Minister are as sanctimonious as can be about the plight of the pensioners when they say that their plight is right next to their hearts, except that many other things come in between when it comes to legislation.
Let me come back to the matter of the servicemen. There seems to be a consistent effort to meld the servicemen's pension funds with the civil service pension funds. There are some good reasons why servicemen prefer that this not happen. It is particularly noticeable when we hear the Canadian Forces

December 6, 1982

Superannuation Act and the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act treated as if the beneficiaries were exactly the same. Elowever, if one looks at the figures, it is quite alarming to servicemen and ex-servicemen because the Forces fund is in a much sounder condition than the supplementary benefits fund.
According to the report on the administration of the Public Service Superannuation Act, there was a balance on 31 March 1981 of $12.7 billion, with 308,000 public servants contributing to it. The Canadian Forces Superannuation Fund stood at $9,327 billion, with only 80,000 contributors. It is obvious from the number of contributors that the servicemen have a much larger vested interest in the superannuation account than the civil servants have. Both accounts seem to be running into difficulty as a result of what the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) is doing today. The Government is treating the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act as if it were the same as the other fund. There is now approximately $25 billion in the two funds. By doing a little bit of arithmetic you will see that the interest on $25 billion would more than pay the entire pensions for both the servicemen and the civil servants.
1 have another grievance. 1 have a letter dated March, 1982, addressed to me which mentions interest. It is from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne). I understand that interest is never paid on these funds. Instead, a paper transaction is made. In 1980 to 1981, the last year for which we have records, the Government in the first quarter "paid" 2.05 per cent on this money. In the second quarter, it "paid" 2.09 per cent; in the third quarter, the amount was 2.01 per cent, and in the fourth quarter, the Government "paid" 2.15 per cent for the money that in theory was in the account. That comes to an annual rate of 8.6 per cent. Everyone knows that the interest rates in 1980 to 1981 were much greater than that.
If we take a look at the amount of interest that was credited to the Canadian Forces Superannuation Fund during that fiscal year, we see that on March 31 the amount credited was $131 million. In the actuarial liability account there is another $348 million, which comes to a total of $479 million. The payments made by Canadian Forces personnel amounted to $80 million. The payments out of the fund were only $280 million in 1980-1981 out of the total amount received of payments of $559 million. Yet we are told the fund is in desperate straits, that it is likely to go broke, and everyone is worried about it. 1 will tell Hon. Members who is worried about it. The servicemen are worried about it because they are the only ones who seem to be able to see money actually going into it. It goes right out of their pay and into the fund and then it goest off in strange directions. Some of it goes to the Canadian Forces superannuation account and some to the actuarial liability account. Servicemen certainly do not know what that is, but in their opinion they do not seem to be getting credit for the money that is in there.
1 was rather surprised when the President of the Treasury Board suggested that he would do a couple of things because of
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
the pressure which had been put on him by some MPs. First, he would raise the cap from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent and then, the following year, it would rise from 5 per cent to 5.5 per cent. Anyway, it was very strange to hear his remark that anyone drawing the Guaranteed Income Supplement would not be severely capped. I am a bit puzzled as to just how this relates to the pay of servicemen or public servants, because I am sure the President of the Treasury Board realizes full well that if one is receiving any kind of pension amounting to $250 a month, except for a disability pension, one cannot qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement. One cannot receive anything from that fund. 1 thought that dragging in that red herring was a little bit beneath the President of the Treasury Board, as only a very few civil servants would ever draw the Guaranteed Income Supplement, I would hope.
The other matter is that this afternoon the President of the Treasury Board announced that those whose pensions were being paid from the Consolidated Revenue Fund would not be eligible for the increased cap, as I understood it. 1 realize that it is a little difficult to follow all these different terms, but if that is so, that would mean that the President of the Treasury Board is penalizing those people who drew pensions before indexation came about. There will be a slight penalty. That is the way it seemed to me. If I am wrong, and if someone from the Government has the gumption to speak in this debate besides the Minister, I will be pleased to hear about it, but that is the way it sounded to me. I see the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary nodding their heads, so I will look forward to hearing how that will be corrected.
References to the pension index make interesting reading. If we consider the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, one finds that this was a promise, really a contract reached with servicemen and public servants, when they were told in 1974 that they would receive their indexed pension. It states:
"Pension Index", with respect to any year, means the average for that year of the Consumer Price Index for Canada, as published by Statistics Canada under the authority of the Statistics Act, for each month in the twelve-month period ending on the thirtieth day of September in the immediately preceding year;
That is a contract, it seems to me, that the pension will be indexed, and the amount by which the pension will be increased. That was the agreement. At that time, servicemen were paying half of one per cent of their pay to cover the cost of indexation. It was found at that time that they needed more money, and it was determined that from then on they would pay a full percentage point. Therefore, servicemen are now paying 7.5 per cent, 6.5 per cent going toward the Force's Superannuation Fund, and 1.5 per cent, I believe, for participation in the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan, and then 1 per cent for the supplementary retirement benefit.
I might point out that because the cost of living and the consumer price index were increasing each year, pensioners were always behind because the pension contribution was

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (A'o. 2)
determined from September to September. If the rates rose 7 per cent, for example, five years ago and 10 per cent four years ago, there was a 3 per cent difference which the pensioner had to pick up because he was paying the charges for that particular year.
1 can briefly indicate some of the figures. If we consider the figures for 1971, one finds that the benefit index was 104 per cent. In 1972 it was 106.5 per cent. That amounted to a 2.5 per cent raise. Therefore, in 1972-73, pensioners would receive an extra 2.5 per cent. However, in 1973, the cost of living rose by 5 per cent. In 1974 it rose by 7 per cent and in 1975 it rose by 12 per cent. Every year the increase given to pensioners was only based on the previous year's increase in the cost of living. Consequently, they were robbed a little bit each year. However, that does not seem to have bothered the Government. Now, strangely enough, when the rate of inflation is beginning to come down, the Government wants to tell them what the benefit index will be in advance. When it was rising, they were paid according to the last year's increase. Now the Government will decide what it will be ahead of time. Next year it will be 6 per cent and the following year it will be 5 per cent, so the Government will get them going both ways.
These figures are spelled out right on the back page of Bill C-133. If one considers the benefit index under column II, one can take the amount of SI,000, one month's pension, and compute what the benefit would be in 1984. One can divide 275.69 by 262.56 and multiply by $1,000 and arrive at an amount of $ 1,050, which is a 5 per cent increase. If inflation is more than that percentage, it is just too bad. One is only a pensioner, anyway, according to the hard-line attitude of the Government. The Government says, "We are sorry we made an awful mess out of running the country, but you have to pick up the cost". It is easy for Hon. Members opposite to say, but it is very hard for them to look people in the eye and tell them that they are doing it to them.
I have in my hand the eleventh annual report on the administration of the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. It was submitted to His Excellency, the Right Hon. Edward Schreyer, Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of Canada, by the President of the Treasury Board. 1 would simply like to point out how this has been arranged according to the Treasury Board which supervised. The Act, if this Bill is approved, will apply to some 26 different acts and groups of people, including the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act as well as the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act which, to my understanding, is now almost non-existent because people have gradually faded out of it.
At page 2 of the report, it states:
The amount of this increase in any January is equal to the percentage increase in the average of the Consumer Price Indices for the twelve months ending on the preceding September 30 over the average for the twelve months ending a year earlier.
In reference to financial provisions, it states:
Between April 1, 1970 and December 31, 1976 employees contributed 16 of 1 per cent of salary. Effective January 1, 1977 this rate was increased to I per cent.
This puzzles me. The Government is attempting to claim that the pension fund, amounting to $25 billion; is not sufficient to pay pensions. I suppose that would be hard to prove to a mortgage company. However, if that is not sufficient, I wonder if the Government has ever thought of asking the people if they are willing to contribute more. In the last couple of months I have spoken with many servicemen and retired and employed civil servants. Most of them would be quite willing to pay another half of one per cent if that were enough, or if it were important. However, they have said, "For God's sake, do not leave us high and dry so that we do not know what will happen in the way of inflation. It would appear that if the rate of inflation keeps on rising, we are the ones who will not become adjusted to it, and we would be willing to contribute". That thought occurred to people in 1977 and they did double their contributions at that time, but it has apparently not been considered at this time.
I would like to point out one other matter. The report continues:
Prior to January 1, 1974, the Act also provided that all supplementary benefits would be charged to the Account. Since that date, however, those benefits paid in respect of a former contributor are charged to the Account only until their accumulated total equals the aggregate of all amounts credited to that Account in respect of that person. Supplementary benefits paid in excess of that aggregate are then charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
This is quite true. These are almost identical words to those found in the Act in Section 8(2), which is of interest. However, Section 9 states:
There shall be credited to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Account in each fiscal year an amount representing interest on the balance from time to time to the credit of the said Account calculated at such rate as may be fixed by the Treasury Board.
We all know how miserly the Treasury Board has been with the interest they have paid on the alleged funds, that they allege are somewhere. 1 expect the President of the Treasury Board has that $25 billion earmarked for somewhere, but there might be people who are not quite as trusting as I am who might wonder if there is any part of it around. I believe the Government made a commitment during the collection and the putting together of those funds, so that the Government actually would consider that the pensioners had a vested interest and were entitled to be consulted and to get a fair deal.
The fund is growing so rapidly, and wording such as this, that the supplementary benefits paid in excess cf the aggregate are then charged to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, is looked on by the pensioner as an effort by the Government to prove that it has paid them back everything they paid in and an indication that it has no further real responsibility, and it is just out of the generosity of the Government heart that it is paying them anything extra from then on. This is what worries the pensioner because he suspects this kind of legislation is really there to take away any rights that ne has to the contract he thought he had with the Government.
December 6, 1982

I can never quite understand how the interest rates are worked out on this, but they seem to me to be much less than they should be.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to point out that these funds have grown so enormously that the Government is neither going to write them out a cheque for it nor set up another fund of an equal size to be self-administered, or in any part administered, by the people who contribute to it, and the people who expect to benefit from it.
I suggested to a meeting of long service pensioners of the Canadian Forces, that perhaps they should try to get this on a sounder footing over a long period of time, say ten or 15 years. If the Government would guarantee to maintain the contract it has with the pensioners, paying them an indexation rate equal to the inflation rate, perhaps the pensioners would be willing to give up any real or imagined right to part of that $25 billion. They accepted that and indicated that if during that ten or 15 year period their contributions and the Government's contributions went into a fund, for instance in the form of Government bonds, which really are much more liquid than the imaginary kind of money being dealt with now, in about ten or 15 years they then would be able to have a funded fund, which is really what the civil servants want and what the Armed Forces want.
In closing, I simply say this is a Bill that I never thought I would see presented in Parliament; that the Government would try to balance its books-which is almost unheard of for this Government-and it would, first of all, pick out old age pensioners and, secondly, those people who thought they had a Government pension. Most of the people who are now retired are people who served their country in the Armed Forces. When they came back from overseas they decided they would stay on in the Forces partly, and to quite a degree, because there was a pension. Nobody ever dreamed of the inflation this Government has brought on in the last 20 years. Pensions had a lot to do with decisions being made by people to stay in Government service. The pay was not as good and the conditions were at times terrible. There were many other disadvantages to being in the Armed Forces, such as being posted at a moment's notice, and the necessity of having one's family educated in a variety of locations. The decision to stay in Government service was made because of the security that Government employment was supposed to offer.
It is shocking to think that the Government would have misled servicemen over the years and then simply, because of its mismanagement of the economy, put their contributions into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and now acts as if they were just a drain on the taxpayer that should not be there at all, when in fact it gives no credence to these figures, figures that are quoted quite frequently by Ministers of the Crown.
A letter from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Famontagne) to me on February 25, 1982 said:
The balance in the account-
That is the superannuation account.
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
-as of 30 September 1981 was $9.89 billion.
He says that it is in there. Who does it belong to? The President of the Treasury Board thinks it belongs to him. There are quite a few people who think it belongs to the serving servicemen and the retired servicemen.
I would hope that the Fiberals, particularly those who represent their constituents in this area, and in other areas as well, might see what a shabby deal they are pulling here. They take a contributory pension, on which a recipient has no say either as to how much he contributes or how often he has to contribute to it, or how often it may be raised without his permission, and summarily decide that they will not give them the payout that had been promised. 1 can simply say that if any organization other than this Government did it there would be a class action lawsuit about it. In fact, I would not think that would be too bad an idea for the veterans to do so right now. When 1 say veterans, I mean the long service pensioners, I do not mean the disability pensioners that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Campbell) might talk about.
I am sorry that the Minister of National Defence is not here at the present time. I had expected he would take part in this debate to support the 80,000 servicemen who are involved and the 33,000, 34,000 or 35,000 annuitants who are retired from the services and drawing these pensions to which they contributed. Perhaps he will take part in the debate this evening or tomorrow, if he has something to say in defence of those people who are contributing to the safety and security of this country.
