subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (N. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the Bill before us this evening is to limit to 6 and 5 per cent

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
any increase in Public Service pensions. Were it not for this Bill, this increase would come to 11.5 per cent, based on the last year's increase in the consumer price index.

It is important to understand that this is not a Bill on pensions, but a Bill which is part of an economic plan designed to bring down the rate of inflation from the 10 or 11 per cent we have known over the past couple of years to, hopefully, six and five per cent in the coming years. It is extremely important to remember this fundamental fact.
When I hear the criticisms of this Bill by Members opposite, I scratch my head and wonder what it is that they would propose. Do they prefer 10 or 11 per cent inflation? What is their plan of action? How do they propose to get inflation down to a lower level? What ideas do they have? Unless they have some ideas on how to reduce inflation in the manner that we are doing, I say their arguments have no force.
In trying to bring down inflation, there are a number of options the Government could have considered, one of which was mandatory wage and price controls. I have not heard any Members opposite come out in favour of that. Last winter, prior to the introduction of this program by the Government, a number of groups submitted briefs strongly urging that mandatory wage and price controls not be considered.
One brief was submitted by the Business Council on National Issues which represents a number of major employers in this country. It strongly urged the Government not to impose such a system, which we knew in 1974, 1975 on to 1978, because of the constraints that were involved, the administrative difficulties and the bureaucracy required to administer it.
They made a submission to the previous minister of finance during the series of consultations which he undertook in the spring and early summer, suggesting a system of voluntary wage and price controls, which the Government subsequently embarked upon. They included a premise in their suggestion. They felt that by and large Canadians are intelligent people who will respond to reason if presented with a reasonable argument. They felt Canadians would respond to the kind of appeal that would be made to them by the Government setting the example and asking industry to comply with the program voluntarily.
What does the Opposition have to say about that? Do they feel that some other approach would be better? A number of people from industry have supported this program. Members are aware of the industry committee established under the chairmanship of Mr. Sinclair. Since then a great number of companies have adhered to this program.
I want to bring to the attention of the House an article which appeared in yesterday's New York Times. Felix Roha-tyn, a prominent investment banker and chairman of the Municipal Assistance Corporation in New York, which engineered New York City's federal aid package in 1975, speaks of the alternatives to Reaganomics. In an extremely thought-provoking article he talks about the necessity of guarding against a renewal of inflation in the United States
caused by wage settlements in excess of productivity improvement. The article reads in part:
Wage and price controls in an advanced industrial society cannot work for long, and a formal, legislative policy, such as a tax-based incomes policy, is probably neither practical nor fair. However, a change in our labour cost structure has to be examined if low inflation is to co-exist with high growth. The most practical way to approach this would be for all major labour contracts to expire simultaneously every year, with wage increases related to existing economic conditions and current inflation; significant elements of profit-sharing should reward real productivity improvements. We should take a cue from Japan and Germany and have an annual, national wage negotiation involving business, labour and often the government. The result should be keyed to the performance of the economy. This is the practical equivalent of an incomes policy for most of the economy.
He looks at the matter of wage and price controls and he says they cannot work for an extended period of time. He looks at tax based incomes policy, and he says that is impractical as well. He argues for some form of an incomes policy which, I believe, our six and five program will ultimately lead to, where wage increases and salaries will be tied to the increase in productivity of the country or to the increase in the gross national product.
Mr. Rohatyn is not the first to advocate such a policy. Lester Thurow, who is, I believe, the favourite economist of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) has written extensively about such a program. I do not hear the Opposition, though, Mr. Speaker, raising such matters. I do not hear them saying, "Well, yes, this is the kind of policy which should be considered in Canada." I do not hear them discussing the pros and cons of it. They just continue to harp about the so-called injustices in our particular program, and these injustices may very well be more perceived than real. I have to conclude that much of their criticism is, as the Hon. Member for Hull, (Mr. Isabelle), I believe, earlier today said, just pure electioneering. They are just playing to the public and trying to score points. They are criticizing the Government for the sake of criticism and trying to appeal, basically, to the fear of Canadians, rather than trying to arrive at a solution to our problems in a constructive manner.
What has seemed to have escaped the attention of both Opposition Parties is that prices as well have been controlled in this program. We are very well aware of the Government's restrictions as they have applied to companies within federal jurisdiction. They must come before federal regulatory agencies like the Canadian Transport Commission or the CRTC. We are also aware of the example of Bell Canada and the fact that their increase in rates was limited to 6 per cent. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, increases in prices throughout the third quarter, for the three-month period, August, September and October, slowed considerably from 3 per cent to 1.7 per cent in May, June and July. On a monthly basis, inflation in October was
0.6 per cent, and when taken with the 0.5 per cent recorded in each of July, August and September, it is solid evidence that inflation is stabilizing at targeted levels. On an annual basis, inflation in October dropped to 10 per cent from 10.4 per cent in September. This decrease continues the steady downward
December 6, 1982

movement from levels which were above 11 per cent prior to July. We have, therefore, dramatic evidence that our policy is beginning to take hold.
I do not claim, and I do not think anyone in our Government has claimed, that our policy is solely responsible for this decrease in the rate of inflation. It is undoubtedly true that a number of companies, and many thousands of small firms, have been restricting their wage and price increases throughout the recent recession, going back about a year or a year and a half. 1 have met countless shop owners and small businessmen in my constituency and elsewhere who have said to me they have not taken a raise in the past several years. In light of this kind of situation, it certainly would be unconscionable for the Public Service, which is not subject to the same kinds of competitive forces as the private sector, and which does not have to depend on the bottom line or the amount of cash which is in the till at the end of the week or month, to continue to have increases at the rate of 10 per cent or 11 per cent when other sectors of the economy cannot take the same kinds of increases and when many are suffering. Indeed, it really is only logical-the kind of logic, perhaps, which escapes the Members of the Opposition-that the Government impose the same restrictions upon its employees as do many companies in the private sector.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, it is true to say also that our program has had an effect on the private sector. I have spoken to a number of businessmen who have told me that when faced by their employees in the course of the past four or five months who perhaps asked for 12 per cent or 9 per cent or whatever, these companies said, "No, the Government has a policy which we intend to follow. It will be 6 per cent over the course of the coming year."
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention briefly that what we are really asking pensioners to do under this Bill, which has been described as a great hardship for them by Members of the Opposition, is not as great a hardship when you look at the cold, hard facts.

Naturally, Mr. Speaker, no one readily wants to limit increases, but the difference between the amount which the pensioners will get as a result of this 6 and 5 per cent limitation and the 11 per cent they would have received otherwise is practically nil. I figured it out. It amounts to perhaps the price of a pack or half a pack of cigarettes a day. The difference will come to $37 a month in 1983. I am not a cigarette smoker, but as far as I know a pack of cigarettes these days costs about $2. So half a pack of cigarettes costs $1, which is the equivalent of the $37-odd loss incurred by the pensioners under this Bill. In my opinion, half a pack less a day is definitely not something which will create undue hardships for pensioners. It can hardly be labelled a loss since pensioners will in fact get an increase. It will be limited to 6 per cent instead of 11 per cent but, as I pointed out earlier, the rate of inflation has already begun to drop sharply. If we manage to bring it down to 7 or 6 per cent in the coming year, it is obvious that there will be no loss. Quite the contrary, the Canadian economy as a whole will be
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
stronger so that pensioners and all Canadians alike stand to benefit from the upturn.
I am grateful to have had this opportunity to take part in the debate, Mr. Speaker. I hope Hon. Members opposite will take the floor and make more constructive contributions to this important debate.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (N. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-133, which amends the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, is simple in form and substance but its effect is shattering to more than 200,000 retired public servants and Armed Forces personnel across this land. The case for the senior citizens should be established and explained to fair-minded legislators and the Canadian electorate who, after all, will judge our performance in this House of Commons on measures such as this Bill.
Let me deal first with a specific provision of Bill C-133. It applies the Government's six and five policy to retirement allowances of those persons subject to the Public Service Superannuation Act so that regardless of the increase in the cost of living, those people are limited to a 6 per cent increase in 1983 and a 5 per cent increase in 1984. It should be made clear, Mr. Speaker, that the designation of the six and five is arbitrary, even imaginary, and not based on fact or even on an economic forecast. In fact, the economic forecast would indicate that the proper increase for the year 1983 would have been, but for the introduction of Bill C-133, something in the area of an 11.5 per cent increase in pensions payable to retired public servants and members of the Armed Forces. If we were to act on the basis of the prediction made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), who indicated that even he does not expect inflation to be reduced below 8 per cent, we would have that as a standard. But there is no basis for assuming that the inflation rate in 1983 will be 6 per cent or 5 per cent in 1984. It is not even anticipated that this is an achievable goal. So what the Government is doing with this restraint policy is simply acting on an arbitrary figure it sought to impose in order to save the public purse. We have to ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, whether that is fair in the circumstances.
1 want to deal with the matter of inflation in Canada and how this economic evil may be attacked, but first let me consider the justification given by the president of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) when he presented this Bill to us. In explaining the Bill he said that it implements the Government's six and five policy which he claimed has a double-track effect of restraining Government spending while providing additional funds for job creation. Mr. Speaker, if that statement were made in the context of a business or social environment instead of a political context, the Minister would at best be condemned for violating business and social ethics. It is well within the realm of possibility that such an extravagant and misleading claim would be considered fraudulent, but unfortunately of a kind and character that would not be subject to a court of criminal law. Nonetheless, it should and does incense fair-minded people. The fact that the Minister

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
would have the Canadian people believe him when he says he wants to restrain public spending and at the same time spend taxpayers' dollars to create jobs means that his fraud is of a public character. That is what I want to accuse the Minister and the Government of Canada tonight of doing, perpetrating a fraud on the Canadian public. It consists of the fact that the Government is restraining Government expenditure and at the same time it is spending more funds for things which the Government thinks will bring it political credit. 1 can say without fear of contradiction that the Goverment's six and five program constitutes a public fraud.
Let me review the program. You remember the night of June 28 when the then minister of finance introduced his budget in the House of Commons. In describing the world of six and five, he said that Canadians have been suffering from a double digit inflation rate and, unless it was brought into line, Canadians would continue to suffer. So what he proposed to do was to start a restraint program, and he would start it with the Government's own employees, the federal public servants. The Minister knew, when he rose in this House on June 28, that there was abroad in this country the idea that federal public servants were overpaid and underworked. Well, Mr. Speaker, there may be those in the Public Service whose jobs attract a salary beyond the salary they could achieve in the private sector, and there may be those in the Public Service who do not work as hard as they ought to, but to characterize the Public Service of Canada as overpaid and underworked is grossly unfair. In fact, the statistics indicate otherwise. Statistics indicate that in the last five years, between 1977 and 1982, the Public Service increases have been marginally behind the private sector increases. I think any person knowledgeable about salary ranges in the Public Service could establish very easily that in specific areas like engineering the salaries are substantially behind those paid in the private sector. In fact, for a medium range engineer, the salary would be something in the order of $3,000 to $6,000 less in the Public Service than in the private sector.
So one has to ask what basis the Government has for restraining the Public Service in the name of helping the economy of Canada. Even restraint of Public Service salaries and related expenditures would be justified if the Government practised and over-all policy of restraint, but we have reason to believe that Government spending programs have gone onwards and upwards since June 28 when this program was announced. We have seen the Post Office pile up ever larger deficits to the extent of $500 million a year. Canadian National Railways come and tell the House of Commons that their deficit is increasing to a similar extent. The Mirabel Airport continues to pile up huge deficits, week after week, to the extent of over $1 million per week or over $50 million per year. We have write-offs for our national ports to the extent of close to $500 million. The list goes on and on. I will not mention, as 1 have several times in the House already, the $24 million thrown away on the purchase of jets, the $5 million to buy firecrackers to celebrate Canada's birthday, or the amount of
money paid to public servants like Michael Pitfield who received a quarter of a million dollars in a settlement deal.
There is no evidence before us that the Government is serious about restraint. The only evidence is Bill C-133, in which the Government attacks retired public servants by taking from them the benefits built up, in many cases, over a lifetime of service. The Government is trying to tell the public that this is its restraint program; that it is so concerned about the amount of money being spent, it is going to cut back on the money it contracted to pay to public servants, in order to demonstrate how serious the situation is.
In a recent speech at a fund-raising event for the Liberal Party, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) referred to the bad times we are having in Canada and said that it is the worst time since the depression but that we are not to worry, because the worst time can be the best time. What he meant was that in times of adversity Canadians come together, look at themselves, and decide what to do about the problem. That may be true in the federal constituency of Mount Royal with its multimillion dollar homes and its $100,000 and $200,000 plus incomes, but it is not true in many parts of Canada. The worst times are not the best times.
It is a shame and a crime that the Prime Minister of Canada, viewing the situation with which so many Canadians are faced, could make the statement that the worst times are the best times. That is his assessment of the situation. In times of adversity you can see good things in the situation, according to the Prime Minister. 1 wonder if he would think that if he went to the coal mining town of Glace Bay with his colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), to see the devastation being effected in that area by this period of recession and if he saw people not only losing their jobs but the hope and expectation of employment in the future. I wonder if he would say then that the worst times are the best times.
If he went to the Strait of Canso with his colleague, the former minister of finance, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), and saw the devastation there, as a result of the economic recession, would he still say the worst times are the best? I should like to see him in the town of Canso or Port Hawkesbury where they are about to close down the major source of employment, the heavy water plant, telling those people that the worst times are the best times.
What we have to conclude is that the Prime Minister and the Government and, I am afraid, all his colleagues in the Liberal Party, deal entirely in perceptions. They think they can sell deals to the people of Canada and that they do not have to worry about the facts of the situation and do not have to deal with the real people who are suffering, the pensioned off public servants. They think they can just deal with the perception that they are attacking the economic problem in Canada, that the businessmen will cheer and the chambers of commerce
December 6, 1982

across the land will join with them in their restraint policy without examining it.
That is why 1 stand in this House time and time again to tell the people of Canada that there is no restraint policy. The Government is not restraining spending. It has gone up and up and up, to $79 billion while revenues stay at $55 billion, leaving a $26 billion deficit. That is what is wrong with Canada. It is not the public servants nor the retired pensioners. They are not creating inflation in Canada. It is the Gover-nemnt that continues to spend and spend and to borrow money to finance that spending that is causing inflation. It will have to do a lot more than pretend, at the expense of public servants and retired public servants, that it is doing something about it.
What is the Government doing to the public servants of Canada who, many Canadians think, are overpaid and underworked? The average pension paid to more than 200,000 retired public servants and members of the Armed Forces, is $6,900. Michael Pitfield and his buddies retire on a much larger pension. In the length and breadth of the Public Service the average pension is $6,900. This, together with the old age pension, which is under $3,000 per year and is going down as a result of another measure that is before the House, gives an income of $9,000 per year for a retired public servant.
If these public servants received the increase they would normally be entitled to of 11.5 per cent, the increase in their pension would be something in the area of $763, whereas with a cap of 6 per cent they will only receive something in the order of $473. What this Bill will do is take $310 away from
200,000	public servants whose total income, including Old Age Security, is $9,000.
If I thought this measure was going to correct all the economic wrongs in Canada, if I thought it was going to change the course of our economic history, if I thought it was going to do anything for the people of Nova Scotia, British Columbia or the Northwest Territories, then I would support it. Even though we are calling upon retired public servants to make that kind of sacrifice, if it meant something for the greater good of Canada and all Canadians, then I think 1 would support it.
There is no way that anyone on the Treasury benches, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) or the former minister of finance or 600 parliamentary assistants, can convince me that taking approximately $300 away from 200,000 retired public servants, is going to help Canada. How could that action possibly help Canada when the Government throws away $500 million on the post office, $100 million on this program and $100 million on that program and provides pension benefits to one public servant, the Clerk of the Executive Council, Michael Pitfield, of about a quarter of a million dollars?
There is no relationship between what the Government says it will do and what it does. That is beginning to bother not only Members of the Opposition but people all across Canada. They are beginning to realize that the Government talks not only from both sides of its mouth but, can I say, from several sides of its mouth. It always tells a different story and paints a different picture. What is most important, it creates perceptions. The Government of Canada never deals with facts. It
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
never deals with the inflation rate nor with specific economic measures that are designed to reduce the inflation rate. It plays with the perception that if we cut back on public servants benefits, we will cut back on public expenditures. The truth is that payments in respect of Public Service salaries went up by 17 per cent in the year in which the Government announced its restraint program. The justification for that, given by the President of the Treasury Board was that Bill C-133 would implement the Government's six and five restraint program and that it was coupled with a job-creation program.
Unfortunately, when the former minister of finance, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso, announced this great restraint program, he did not mention job creation as being the other side of it. He picked that up later when the Government realized the problem in Canada was not really inflation or high interest rates but was unemployment. It did not find that out until a couple of months later when the unemployment rate went up a couple of points to 1.4 million people uenmployed. Then the Government began to realize that even though the Governor of the Bank of Canada and other high-priced economists did not like the rate of inflation or the interest rate, the real human problem in the country was unemployment. That is when it started to talk about job creation.
In the June 28 budget when the Minister of Finance announced measures the Government would take to cap salaries and incomes in the Public Service, he said that over a two-year period something in the area of $800 million would be saved. He immediately announced expenditures of $2 billion, most of which were directed at small business and some of which were directed at lowering interest rates. Now the Government has come forward with a job creation program in which it will spend $500 million to create 60,000 part-time jobs. It is trying to claim that that program is tied in with the caps on Public Service salaries and with increases in Public Service pensions.
There comes a time when even the Government has to give up trying to fool Members of the House and the people of Canada. If it does not know what it is doing, it can simply come to the Parliament of Canada and say, "We are sorry, ladies and gentlemen, we do not know what we are doing. We have made a number of mistakes in the past but now we want to co-operate with Members of Parliament and with people across Canada to remedy the situation." If the Government took that honest approach, I would have some sympathy for it. I would even be willing to explain to public servants and persons receiving Public Service pensions that they have to contribute in the same way as all Canadians. But that is not what the Government has done. It has simply redirected some of the funds without cutting back on expenditures at all.
Nonetheless, inflation will decrease in Canada. The interest rate will go down and is going down. The reason is that economic activity is grinding to a halt. The reason we will have

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
a lower inflation rate over the next months and years is not the Government's six and five program. The reason is that there is no economic activity in Canada. The reason interest rates will go down is that no one is expanding his or her business or borrowing funds for business purposes, so the demand for money simply goes down. It is the lack of economic activity in Canada which is bringing down the inflation rate and the interest rate, not the Government's six and five program. One does not have to be an economist to recognize that fact.
The real fact in Canada is that there are 1.4 million unemployed persons. There were 55,000 more unemployed people this month over the figure for last month. We have every reason to believe that there will be another 50,000 to 60,000 people unemployed next month. The 1.4 million listed by Statistics Canada does not include all unemployed persons in Canada. There are all the people who have given up looking for work, 250,000 or more. There are all the people who are employed at jobs in levels well below their qualifications, that is another 250,000 to 300,000. There are all the part-time workers, the 800,000 who are working part time, at least half of whom want to work full time. There are not just 1.4 million unemployed. There are over two million or almost 2,5 million persons in Canada with serious employment problems. They are unemployed, have given up looking for work, are working below their job levels or part time. This is the result of the Government's policy. It will not be cured by any six and five restraint program. It will not even be helped by any six and five restraint program. All it does is to give the Government opportunity to take money from one sector of the population and spend it in another sector.
With the Government's record over the past decade of reallocating wealth in the country, it is no wonder that Canadians, particularly Members of Parliament, are wary about giving the Government the right to reallocate any wealth in the country.
Let us look at some of the programs which the Government has created. There is the $3,000 grant to purchasers of new homes and to new home purchasers. On the face of it, it sounds like a reasonable program. It helps owners and it helps stimulate the housing industry. But in the hands of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation the program becomes a complete shambles.
I will not complain about that in the House of Commons because if the Minister of Housing does not know then he should that every recipient, whether the person is a new home purchaser or the purchaser of a new home, is disgusted with the Government before he or she ever receives a cheque. Recipients are disgusted with the Government because of the rigmarole through which they have to go to get the grants, the bureaucracy they have to face, the forms they have to fill out, the actions they have to take and the insults they have to endure from CMHC to obtain $3,000 grants. If the Government expected to get any votes out of the program, I can tell it that it will not.
It is the same situation with the home improvement program under which the Government provided Canadians with nonrepayable loans. Again we see the Government misleading the people. It cannot even call a grant a grant any more. It has to phrase it in some way that is hardly understandable to most Canadians. If Government Members think that is helping them politically, they are mistaken because everyone 1 have talked with who applied for home improvement grants is completely dissatisfied.
In the first place, I do not know of any contractors in Canada to whom one can go, certainly in my part of Canada, Nova Scotia, and expect them to do kitchen work in six months' time. It takes at least six or seven weeks to contact CMHC and arrange for an inspection of one's home, which is a prerequisite to the grant. It does not make any difference what one is doing in the home. If it is something which is clearly visible as home improvement work, a week, a month or six months later one has to have an inspection. Every CMHC office across the country cannot provide inspections for at least five, six or seven weeks. Again there is no connection between the Government's announced policy in the House of Commons and what is taking place out in the country.
It is interesting that I should have an opportunity to say this to Ministers of the Crown. They sit around Cabinet with their advisers in the bureaucracy and dream up these programs without any reference to what is going on in the cities and towns across the country. This time they made a disastrous and dreadful mistake. Whereas they promised to give elderly citizens an extra $35 a month during the election campaign- and I would be the first to admit that it might have brought them a few votes-whereas they promised to provide new home owners and purchasers of new homes with $3,000 grants, and whereas they promised to provide Canadian citizens who wanted to renovate their homes with interest-free loans, the plans have backfired because they are not administering them properly.
Time and time again as part of the Government's economic program to help get the economy moving again, we have heard of help for small businesses. One does not have to talk very long to any small-businessman across the country before finding out that in his or her opinion the Government is doing nothing to help small business. In fact, the complaint is still there that the Government is riding on the backs of small-businessmen. The Government places a burden of regulatory control or a burden of Government regulations which is actually swamping small business across the country. Small businesses which might have coped in good times with this myriad and morass of Government regulations now find the burden too onerous. They do not want to carry on with high interest rates and all other problems which arise from a recessionary period within the economy. Small-businessmen are giving up. When the Government comes forward in the House of Commons saying that it is taking $800 million from public servants to put in a program to help small-businessmen,
I am sure business persons across the country are asking, "Where is the help?" How many are actually seeing this help?
I have talked with a great many small-businessmen. None of
December 6, 1982

them have asked me to thank the Government for providing the help it claims it wants to provide.
I want to deal for a moment with the plight of pensioners across the country. As 1 have indicated, there is the idea that public servants have been overpaid for a long period of time, that they are not required to work as hard or their work is not as difficult as their equivalents in the private sector. It is very difficult to deal with that kind of subjective analysis. All you can do is to show people that in fact Public Service salaries are not as high as equivalent positions in the private sector, which has been proved time and time again by statistical analysis. You can show and demonstrate to person in the private sector that increases in that area have been higher for the last five years, though only marginally higher than increases in the Public Service. But you cannot deal effectively with the perception that really is the situation. You cannot always confront the perception with the facts because people are not willing to listen to facts once they have formed that idea.
1 want to say to the Public Service pensioners across Canada that it is a shame the Government has created this perception and aids and abets it by saying in this House of Commons and elsewhere that we have to cut down on the Public Service both in relation to salaries and benefits to public servants who are now unemployed and in the superannuation payments made to retired public servants. We have to cut down on that expenditure.
At the same time, the Government does not point out the plight of the public servants. The Government does not point out that the average retired public servant receives an income of $6,500. The Government does not point out that in some cases public servants have taken early retirement because their jobs have been abolished. The Government talks about security in the public sector, but there is no security for a public servant in a recessionary period any more than in some aspects of the private sector. You have to be careful when making comparisons here, Mr. Speaker. One cannot compare an employee in the federal Public Service to an employee in some small regional industry that is totally dependent upon the economy of that region or on the state of the business in which the employer is engaged. But if one compares federal public servants to those employed in large organizations in the energy field, such as Imperial Oil, or if one compares federal public servants to employees working for large banks, such as the Royal Bank of Canada, then one can make a fair comparison. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that you will then find that job security is any different among employers at that level.
However, the Government has said, and the Minister of Finance has said in this House of Commons, that public servants should accept less because they have job security and because they have the assurance that they will continue to be employed, and they should share with fellow Canadians who are not employed the benefits of their employment. That makes sense. That is a rational approach to the situation.
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
I think that most Canadians, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in one of his fireside chats, are willing to share. But Canadians want this sharing to be based on real facts. Canadians want this sharing to be based on truth. They want the sharing to be based on the fact that the public servants now employed do have job security. The President of the Treasury Board stood up last week and said that the Government will have to get rid of a lot of public servants, that it is going to have to cut down, because that is part of the program. What he forgot is that there may be 500,000 persons employed in the Public Service and he may be getting rid of only 10,000 or
20,000	but those public servants do not know who he means in that group. They do not know who of the 10,000 to 20,000 will lose his or her employment.
If you think that creates job security among people, Mr. Speaker, and if you think that one does not have to worry because he or she probably will not be the one in the small percentage of public servants who will lose his or her employment, if you think that gives public servants any sense of satisfaction or makes them happy at having spent most of their adult lives in the Public Service, then you are making an awful mistake, Mr. Speaker. One either has job security or one does not have job security. It is not a hit or a miss proposition to have job security. Job security is not based on percentages; it is based on the right to keep your employment against the wishes of your employer. If a person simply has a job at the whim or demand of one's employer, then a person does not have job security.
When you run down the whole list of assets that one gains by employment in the Public Service, and subsequent retirement, you find very quickly that the Government is taking most of the assets away. One has to ask what the Government is providing by way of compensation. What is it doing to make Canada a better place in which to live? What is the Government doing to contribute to economic security in the future? If there were a positive answer to that question, I think everybody in this House of Commons would say that the exercise was worthwhile. If this action that is being taken by the Government will help the economy of Canada and contribute to a better future for all Canadians, then I agree, and 1 am sure most Members would agree, that all Canadians ought to be called upon to share in this venture.
I have not seen any evidence that that will be the result of the Government's program. I cannot see any evidence that what the Government is taking from one sector and giving to another is going to produce anything substantial. 1 believe it is all a facade. 1 believe it is all phony. 1 think the Government is trying to fool Members of the House of Commons, the Parliament of Canada and the people of Canada. I think the Government has come to the end of the line. The Government realizes that it has mismanaged the affairs of Canada to the point where it cannot effectively administer the economy. This Government has overspent, as I have said, to the tune of $26 billion in the current fiscal year. This Government has run up a total debt of $132 billion. The Government has to use over $1 in every $4 in revenue to service that debt. Yet because of a

December 6, 1982
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
situation aggravated by a world-wide problem in trade and business activity, we find ourselves with a gross economic problem.
There is no economic activity in Canada. There is no business income to pay off this debt. There is no money to invest. There is no reason to invest in new activity. Therefore, the Government can no longer depend upon the private sector to bail us out of this situation. What does the Government do? The Government does not call in the private sector and deal with the problem in a realistic way. The Government does not really examine the total process by which it has dealt with the economy. It simply announces a program for which the claim is made that it will resolve the economic problem.
The problem is that the Government's fraud is starting to affect people in a real way. When the Government of Canada comes to the House of Commons for legislative authority to take $1.61 a month away from each child under 18 in Canada; when the Government of Canada comes to the House of Commons for legislative authority to take $300 a year away from retired public servants and thus reduce their income, which is actually only at the $6,000 or $5,000 level; when you find those kinds of measures-not to mention the Bill before the House to deprive persons receiving Old Age Assistance of $19 a year-and you add them up, the children, the senior citizens and the Public Service pensioners who are being asked to contribute millions of dollars to the Government of Canada only to be redirected in some of the ways that I have already pointed out to pay for the massive deficits on the railway system, and the postal service, then you know that we are in trouble.
Even The Toronto Star was forced to write an editorial condemning the Government for its policy with respect to this Bill, Bill C-133. Even The Toronto Star has to question the rightfulness of depriving retired federal public servants of a reasonable increase in their pensions.
I would like to direct the attention of the House to exactly what we are doing here and why we are doing it, because I do not think anyone can seriously justify the breach of a contract embedded in this statutory provision-with the condonation of statutory provisions-in the name of restraint when the real effect of the breach of that contract is simply to transfer Government funds from one group of Canadians to another. In more specific terms, I do not see how the Government of Canada could ever justify breaching its contract with retired public servants and taking dollars out of their pockets unless it is part of an over-all, complete program whereby all public expenditures are limited to the same amount.
However, I have said time and time again that we know public expenditures are not being limited in that way. We know that the Government has no intention of decreasing its payments to people, even those in the employ of the Public Service, and we have seen that time and time again.
Let me close by simply saying that we have before us a Bill which, in effect, is a breach of a sacred contract between the Government of Canada and its retired public servants. The breach of that contract could only be justified on the most extreme grounds, and those grounds simply do not exist in this case. The action of the Government is wrong and I do not see how anyone in the House can properly support it.

Indexing does not give pensioners an increasingly larger claim on our economy's production, that is, more money to buy things they could earlier afford. Rather, indexing merely enables pensioners to maintain, roughly, their same standard of living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to say a few words on Bill C-133. It is interesting to note that some of the Members across the way are making comments tonight that they see no reason to believe that inflation will come down during the next 12 months. Yet, if we look at the inflation rate since the six and five program was introduced on June 28, we would see that the inflation rate for each of the months, July, August and September, was in fact 0.5 per cent which, annually, comes out to exactly 6 per cent. In October it was 0.6 per cent. So it is hovering right around the 6 per cent annual rate which, 1 believe, is really encouraging and, I am sure, indicates the kind of support that there has been for this program.
I know that the Members in the Opposition do not like to see that much support for the six and five program. They are used to Gallup polls which go in another direction. But, clearly, the public support for the six and five program has been very encouraging, and the results, as far as inflation is concerned, are very encouraging. If we look at the Gallup poll taken I believe in September of this year, some 64 per cent of respondents said that they supported the program, some 67 per cent said they wanted to see the restraint program extended to provincial Governments, and 63 per cent felt the ceiling should also apply to the private sector. Another poll which was conducted by The Toronto Star of 200 Metropolitan Toronto residents in August found that 50 per cent of the full-time employed Torontonians were willing to accept a 6 per cent limit on their wage increases. Asked about the extension of federal guidelines to various employee groups, 83 per cent said they should apply to provincial and municipal employees, 75 per cent to employees of large corporations, 74 per cent to construction workers, 71 per cent to the medical profession, and 61 per cent said that they themselves should be governed by the 6 per cent guidelines. This program, of course, is at the federal level and is only compulsory for federal Government civil servants and Crown Corporations representing some
500,000	employees, but it is interesting that when the provincial Premiers came together this summer, although they were not really agreeable to it then, some seven out of the ten
provincial Governments now have adopted some kind of restraint program.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the voluntary approach of the private sector is more desirable than a compulsory approach, because it seems to me that many unions and many collective bargaining agreements which were reached, say, last summer or the previous summer, and are in effect for a period of two or three years, even though they were well beyond the six and five guidelines, the economic circumstances demand and have resulted in a much tighter, more efficient, more productive shop situation.
I have heard recently of a large industry where there have been quite heavy lay-offs, where the demand for their products is not very great, where they have had to bring in tremendous efficiencies, and where previously a shop would have maybe 20 people working in it, they have now honed it down to 12 or 13 workers. In fact, they are putting in place a very austere and restrained work situation even though they have a collective agreement which runs over a three-year period and which is far above the six and five guidelines.
A Member across the way complained that the problem, Mr. Speaker, was really high unemployment and lack of jobs, not inflation. Well, it is both. The six and five program is designed to address both, because not only does it try to reduce inflation to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the year after- and it is looking very encouraging in that regard-but the money saved, some $750 million, principally in wages, over that two-year period is being allocated to job creation.
In my own constituency we have been able to announce a number of Canada Community Development Projects, I believe about 40 or 50, resulting in several hundred jobs this coming winter at a cost of over $1 million. That is considerably more than we were able to provide last year, and for an area like mine in northern Ontario where we have high seasonal unemployment, those job creation funds are very much needed and will be very beneficial this coming winter. But that is only one part of the Canada Community Development Project. It has a special feature for native people and for young unemployed Canadians. I am really pleased about that because if you look at the unemployment statistics, they reflect a very high level of unemployment among young people. In addition, there is a fund of $18 million under this Program for native peoples.
Last Friday morning, Mr. Speaker, I had the opportunity to attend a signing ceremony with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), along with the Ontario Treasurer, Mr. Frank Miller, and the Ontario Minister of Labour, Mr. Russ Ramsay. The agreement signed will put in place some $200 million, the federal share of which, $100 million, is reallocated funds from other sectors of the federal Government. That shows that the over-all thrust of the six and five program is toward restraint in the federal Government, while at the same time reallocating Government funds to
December 6, 1982

create jobs. I would just point that out to the Hon. Member across the way who said that the concern must be for jobs. Surely, when we are implementing direct employment programs, they should ultimately result in jobs in the private sector. I have a project in my constituency which we have been trying to get going for the last six months or year. It is to create a new shipping terminal to ship aggregates and sand to the United States. The markets are not too great right now, but as we come out of the recession in the next year or so there will be tremendous markets in the U.S. It is those kinds of programs or ventures which we should be putting in place because, after all, it is the private sector which generates the taxes which pay for the social security system we have in this country. So I think it is important that as we go about creating jobs, we create an infrastructure within the private sector which will create long-term jobs. That is really important.
I think it is also important, Mr. Speaker, even though this program is compulsory for MPs and civil servants, that we give leadership. I think the rollback in MPs wages was a good signal to the private sector in that regard. Although it is voluntary in the private sector, the compulsory aspect for federal employees is seen as a clear signal. I think the private sector has been responding in a tremendously positive and creative way, labour as well as management, in an effort to make industry more competitive, more productive and efficient.
I spoke recently with the president of a large corporation who said that whenever they discussed with their employees the idea of more productivity or improving the quality of workmanship, or greater efficiency, their response was pretty negative and along the lines of, well, the company is making lots of money, why should we worry about productivity? Yet during these past six months, when we have really been under the gun for markets, for opportunities for our products, and when everything is so tremendously competitive, that attitude has changed. Labour is saying, yes, how can we make the industry more productive, how can we keep those markets overseas, how can we co-operate and work together? That is one of the benefits of this situation.
There is not a lot that we can do to create new markets overseas, which are so important to a resource-producing area like my own, but we can put in place a very efficient and lean industry, one able to face that kind of competition with wage settlements comparable to those in the U.S. and our other trading partners so that we can have products which will compete in the world market. This Bill before us tonight, Bill C-133, is one part of that effort.
.
It can be argued that these employees, whether they are former MPs or civil servants, have a contract under which they contributed 1 per cent of their salaries in order to have full indexation-and I understand the Government matched that-and that they should not be restrained in any way. If we look at the over-all picture in the country, old age pensioners and people receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement who
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
do not have much or perhaps not even any Canada Pension Plan benefit, are restrained to six and five. I was pleased that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) indicated that those full contributions, that 1 per cent from the employee and 1 per cent from the employer, would be passed on and that the only thing that would be restrained, in effect, was that part of the indexation which comes directly from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
Surely if we are successful in reducing inflation-and the first four months of the program are very encouraging in that regard in many sectors of the economy such as food, transportation, housing and so on-and if we get it down close to 6 or 7 per cent in 1983, then the pensioner who would be affected by the Bill would only be so affected to a minimum degree. We hope that the restraint on inflation will continue and that it will come down to 5 per cent in the following years.
The cost of energy has had the effect of pushing inflation up in the past few years. It is interesting that a couple of weeks ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) announced that next year's increase will be minimal, and that the compensation fund increases will be reduced. That will compensate for the increases coming as a result of the Canada-Alberta Agreement.
When the six and five program was announced in late June, many senior citizens receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement and Old Age Security-not pensioners who would be affected by this Bill-spoke out and said they wanted to play their part. If we all play our part in trying to reduce inflation to 6 per cent next year, then people receiving 6 per cent or 6.5 per cent as indicated in the Bill, will suffer considerably less than they might have otherwise.
Those are a few thoughts that I think should be placed on the record, Mr. Speaker. The six and five program is designed to restrain benefits to federal civil servants and, as well, to create employment for this coming winter. It will probably be the worst winter since the 1930s as far as unemployment is concerned. Industries that are still operating and producing jobs have tended to tighten their belts and employ a minimum of staff.
I think we have to work together, the private sector, Government and industry, and use all the tools available to us. Whether it is the new program for employment and economic development to create jobs in the private sector or the program to create employment for forestry workers, there must be a coming together of all forces at all levels of Government.
During the past three or four months we have seen great cooperation between the private sector, municipal Governments and provincial Governments, not only to create jobs through the funds being made available by the six and five program, but to do worthwhile things in the community. The six and five program has been successful in giving people an objective to work toward rather than demanding high amounts of money at a time when the economy simply cannot afford it. I think there is an opportunity through the program to create jobs, to limit

1 think we should support this program. The inflation rate is coming down, interest rates are coming down and there is the prospect for greater growth next year. subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-AIR CANADA LAY-OFFS-APPLICATION OF EARLY RETIREMENT POLICY TO MACHINISTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MEDIATOR BE APPOINTED
LABOUR CONDITIONS-AIR CANADA LAY-OFFS-APPLICATION OF EARLY RETIREMENT POLICY TO MACHINISTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MEDIATOR BE APPOINTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I directed a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) regarding the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers of Air Canada being informed that 585 employees of that group will be laid off. I asked whether the Minister would inquire as to why Air Canada is not willing to apply its voluntary separation program to the machinists and aerospace workers, as it is doing to management personnel and employees of other bargaining units in the Air Canada family.
The Minister of Transport answered by indicating that in the case of management people the separation was a permanent one, and that they were not subject to recall or the protection of collective agreements. He also indicated that in the case of machinists they were subject to recall and were protected by collective agreements in terms of pensions.
The Minister said that the cases of the management people and the machinists were quite different. Why then was Air Canada prepared at one time to offer machinists the same basic program, although not nearly as beneficial to machinists as the one it offered management?
I should also like to point out that under the presidency of Claude Taylor, Air Canada has become one of the most efficient and well-managed airlines in the world. But serious labour problems have arisen in Air Canada with the proposed lay-off of 585 machinists. 1 hope Mr. Taylor will personally intervene and work toward a satisfactory solution, as has been the case with other Air Canada groups.
Also, Air Canada could be violating Sections 7 and 10 of the Canadian Human Rights Act by not treating all employee groups in the same manner. I am prepared to file a claim with the Canadian Human Rights Commission if this situation is not corrected. I hope I do not have to take those steps.
December 6, 1982

The International Association of Machinists is distributing cards across Canada which read:
As an Air Canada worker, my wages are being controlled under the six and five program. That's for the good of the country, so I'm told.
Now, Air Canada is threatening me with lay-off if I don't concede some of my existing benefits. That's JOB BLACKMAIL.
At the same time, the Company is offering a $21 million "Golden Handshake'' deal to its management personnel. That's downright discrimination.
The Air Canada voluntary separation program is an early retirement program designed selectively to trim management staff with a minimum of hardship for the employee. On August 30, 1982, Air Canada offered a voluntary separation program to its existing management staff levels due to economic conditions. This program will cost approximately $21 million, to be paid from the company's operating fund.
Meanwhile, on September 7, 1982, the union met with Air Canada to discuss the company's plan with regard to staff reductions of the International Association of Machinists across Canada. The company indicated that the total machinists group would be reduced by approximately 518 people. At that time the position taken by the union was to extend to the International Association of Machinists the voluntary separation program being offered to all management personnel. The company's reaction was that this was out of the question.
On September 24, 1982, Air Canada discussed with the union the possibility of the voluntary separation program for the International Association of Machinists but presented to them a substantially reduced program than the one being offered to management. The cost of including the IAM members in such a program would be approximately $3 million, and the union would have to make concessions for an equivalent $3 million to offset this program, which does not even compare to the benefits being offered to management. This could be a violation of Section 7 and Section 10 of the Canadian Human Rights Act. The company is voluntarily spending $21 million for management apparently, with no strings attached.
In a letter to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) dated September 24, 1982, from Air Canada, it was stated that layoffs from the International Association of Machinists would total 585 employees, not 518 as originally assumed. In the meantime, employees of other bargaining units in the Air Canada family have obtained the voluntary separation program.
On September 30, 1982, the company informed the union that if it is ready to accept certain concessions the company's committee would try to get approval for a voluntary separation program. On October 8, 1982, the union informed the company that it was willing to submit to its members the company's offer for ratification. The company replied that the offer no longer existed. On October 19, 1982, a letter was sent to the Minister of Transport requesting assistance. Just recently an acknowledgement has been received, but it was not a satisfactory one.
Adjournment Debate
The International Association of Machinists feels that with a voluntary separation plan, similar to what management personnel is receiving, the number of machinists who will be laid off effective January 3, 1983, and April, 1983, could be substantially reduced from the 585 total, therefore easing the burden on unemployment insurance.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will inform us tonight that the Government will intervene and try to get the two parties together. Let us try to come up with the same voluntary plan and the same satisfactory solution for the machinists as Air Canada has been providing to management personnel and other groups within Air Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-AIR CANADA LAY-OFFS-APPLICATION OF EARLY RETIREMENT POLICY TO MACHINISTS. (B) REQUEST THAT MEDIATOR BE APPOINTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the tasks I take very seriously in Parliament is my role as Chairman of the Helsinki Parliamentary Group on Human Rights. If an individual Canadian or a certain group of Canadians were being discriminated against, as the Hon. Member charges, I would be the first Member in this House to fight for the protection of their rights.
Let us look at some of the facts surrounding the charges against Air Canada made by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie).
Air Canada is using almost 15 per cent more manpower today to accomplish the same workload it performed five years ago. To remain competitive, it must reduce its scale of operations to match the traffic available. Faced with the prospect of lay-offs, Air Canada has examined and proposed various alternative ways of achieving the necessary cost reductions. For example, Air Canada pilots were offered, and overwhelmingly accepted, a five per cent reduction in flying time, which roughly corresponds to a 5 per cent cut in pay. I congratulate the pilots on their wisdom and co-operation in helping to solve a real problem.
The International Association of Machinists and aerospace workers, to which the Hon. Member referred, were offered the comprehensive package which included worksharing, leaves of absence and a voluntary separation settlement. 1 emphasize that the machinists were offered a form of voluntary separation settlement. Granted, it was not the same as that offered to management, and rightly so, because the union is protected by the security of the collective agreement, whereas a laid-off management employee is permanently separated from the company. The International Association of Machinists rejected the comprehensive package. This is regretted by Air Canada and by the Government as this package would have allowed Air Canada to retain many, if not all, of the employees without seniority which it is now being forced to lay off. However, those lay-offs are entirely within the terms of the collective agreement.
Laid off employees and contract groups generally remain employees of the company, retain certain rights and are guaranteed return to their jobs when work becomes available.

In my view, this can hardly be described as discrimination against a certain group of employees, as unfairly charged by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine.

subtopic: MINES AND MINING-UNION RECOMMENDATIONS ON STOCKPILING. (B) RESTORATION OF COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE
MINES AND MINING-UNION RECOMMENDATIONS ON STOCKPILING. (B) RESTORATION OF COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 1, as reported at page 20232 of Hansard, I raised questions of the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) and the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) with regard to the very seriously deteriorated state of Canada's mineral industry.
Canada's mining industry produces some $10 billion of net benefits to Canada's gross national product and balance of payments because a large proportion of our minerals produced is exported, in excess of 80 per cent. As we have seen in the past year, most of Canada's major mining companies have had to exercise substantial lay-offs amounting to lost employment for thousands of mine workers across Canada, and in resource communities in particular, which depend heavily on mining operations as the mainstay of their economies. 1 am thinking of the asbestos mining industry of Quebec, the iron ore industry of Labrador, Northern Ontario and Quebec, the nickel industry in the Sudbury area, the uranium industry, the potash industry and the lead and zinc industries, as well as the mining activities in the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia.
The questions really focused on determining whether or not the Ministers responsible had come to recognize the tragic deterioration of Canada's competitive position in international markets. To consider the nickel industry alone, for a moment, it is now known that there are some 25 other competing nations producing nickel, while in 1950 Canada was one of the world's three leading nickel producers. We have now developed a major industry in Sudbury, primarily represented by Inco and Falconbridge, which employ in excess of 15,000 workers, but that industry is only active to the extent of 38 per cent of its capacity. In fact, the world nickel industry is only performing at 57 per cent of total capacity.
The question 1 asked the Ministers was whether or not they had addressed this serious problem and had some solutions to offer. It has been recognized for some time that this problem did not just occur during the last 12 months. As pointed out in a brief to the Government earlier this year from the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Mines, Canada's share of metal mining markets has been in a state of decline for the past ten to 15 years. In fact, statistically speaking, we have seen our share of the world nickel market, for example, reduced from 75.7 per cent in 1950 to only 25 per cent in 1980. The Chamber of Mines, in identifying this problem, singled out the Minister of State for Mines and her policy discussion paper released last March, which totally failed to address this
problem of Canada's deteriorating competitiveness and the world market situation. The brief states:
Ignoring the decline in Canadian mineral production and independent studies that are critical of past federal policies has reduced the credibility of the Mineral Policy Discussion Paper. This deficiency must be corrected at once before it affects discussions with the provincial governments.
I would like to state some of the reasons Canada's competitive position has failed so miserably.
First of all, one of our most important customers for mineral resources is the United States of America which purchased more than 50 per cent of Canada's non-fuel mineral exports in 1980. The anti-American policies of this Government, both in terms of defence and security, but more particularly as represented by the National Energy Program, and our anti-investment policies with respect to foreign and American investment, have had a very detrimental impact on our potential for sales of minerals to the American market.
I want to point out, in case the Parliamentary Secretary is concerned, that the B.C. and Yukon Chamber of Mines say that it is not the current slump in the international marketplace that is at fault, but the vicious and deteriorating problem that has been developing over many years which cannot be ascribed to the current economic downturn.
In addition to the anti-American policies have been the antiinvestment policies and the tendency to protectionism of the present Government which has driven away many Japanese purchasers of minerals. If we do not want to purchase cars built in Japan, they have less desire to buy our coal. They have therefore cut back on their coal imports by 30 per cent in the past year. They are buying less lead and zinc, therefore Cyprus Anvil and the northern mines are going down. They are buying less iron ore, and therefore the iron ore industry of northern Quebec is in trouble.
What I am saying in a nutshell is that the anti-investment policies, the discriminatory and volatile tax policies of this Government, the high energy taxation and the lack of regard for our important trading partners are at the heart of this serious dilemma. I would be pleased to see what response the Government members have to offer to this very serious problem which is affecting thousands and thousands of mine workers across Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: MINES AND MINING-UNION RECOMMENDATIONS ON STOCKPILING. (B) RESTORATION OF COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the Hon. Member's concern, I must say that we on this side of the House are also very concerned about the situation.
The Hon. Member raises the question of stockpiling nickel, as did the Steelworkers Union in Sudbury last week when they met with the Leader of the Conservative Party of Canada. The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) described the proposition of stockpiling as "intriguing" and that his Party will "seriously examine it." He said, and I quote, "it makes sense". Serious examination will show that nickel is only one of our metals experiencing a world slump in prices; so
December 6, 1982

also is copper, zinc, lead, silver and iron ore, just to name a few.
With the exception of cement, Canada exports the major portion of its mining output, and must accept world market prices. Stockpiling not only upsets this world market even more, it is outrageously expensive. When markets recover it is very difficult to dispose of stockpiles.
Estimates have been made on a case-by-case basis of the costs of bringing operations that are temporarily closed back into production, but time does not allow a detailed examination of those here. Let it suffice to say that for a nickel stockpiling program alone, which would stockpile the difference between the amount of nickel produced in Canada in 1982, and 1981, which were not banner years for that industry, it would cost the Canadian taxpayers about half a billion dollars, using a nickel price which would only cover the producer's operating costs. This does not include those mines still open, but operating at a loss, who might also want assistance, particularly as their losses would be aggravated by the depressing effect of increased inventories. That is not to say that this Government does not care about the people in the Sudbury basin.
The Hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) has been meeting regularly with all levels of Governments, with the unions and the companies, to come up with some creative solutions to this very disturbing unemployment situation. It ought to be mentioned that the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) has been actively pursuing creative solutions to rectify a very, very difficult situation caused primarily by a world economic recession.

subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED FUTURE OF NOVA SCOTIA HEAVY WATER PLANTS. (B) POLICY ON SALES TO INDIA
ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED FUTURE OF NOVA SCOTIA HEAVY WATER PLANTS. (B) POLICY ON SALES TO INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin my remarks by pointing out to the House that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited operates in the Province of Nova Scotia two heavy water plants respectively located at Glace Bay and at Port Hswkesbury in the Strait of Canso. These two heavy water plants have been in operation for several years and employ jointly over 700 persons directly, and probably another 2,000 persons indirectly. Therefore, any cessation of the operation of these heavy water plants would result in a loss of jobs in the area of 3,000 persons in the Cape Breton area of Nova Scotia.
I would point out that that area of Cape Breton now has an unemployment rate of approximately 19.5 per cent. There is no question that if the operation of these heavy water plants in Cape Breton was endangered and if they were to cease operation, there would be a very serious problem created on top of the existing serious unemployment problem in the Island of Cape Breton which would affect the economy of the whole of Nova Scotia.
With that in mind, on November 3, 1982 1 rose in the House of Commons and asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), and subsequently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), what action might be taken to ensure the
Adjournment Debate
continued operation of these heavy water plants by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. On that day I was not successful in obtaining a clear and careful answer to my inquiry. Although the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources did indicate there was a serious problem with the marketing of the Candu reactor both in domestic and international terms and the failure to sell Candu reactors domestically and internationally would mean there was no market for the heavy water to fuel these plants.
Given the problem with the Candu reactor program, in that it has been unsuccessful, I still want to ask the Government what it proposes to do in the face of this horrendous problem in Cape Breton Island and across the Province of Nova Scotia. What in a word is the solution?
1 do not believe, and 1 am sure my colleague from Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) does not believe the economy of Cape Breton and Nova Scotia can withstand this tremendous amount of unemployment which, beyond the persons immediately affected, would have a disastrous effect on the operation of the power plants that are related to the operation of the heavy water plants at Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury. In addition, there is a vast amount of coal produced in connection with these operations that would be left without a market, as well as the effect on the miners who engage in that operation.
In search of a solution the employees of the heavy water plants have made the suggestion that the Government should consider the construction of three 600-megawatt Candu reactors in Canada to be related to other energy projects. They point out in graphic terms that this could be of great assistance to the energy industry across Canada because the reactors could be used to fuel and assist broader energy projects.
Those employees of the heavy water plants pointed out in very clear terms that the economic activity generated by the operation of the heavy water plants is a very serious concern because they pump a vast amount of money into the economy. In fact, it was indicated by Atomic Energy of Canada that the cost to that organization of operating the heavy water plants is in excess of $ 120 million per year.
One wonders what the obligation is of the Government of Canada in this situation. Let me refer to a remark by the Prime Minister made in June of this year when the unemployment rate had risen to 10.8 per cent. He said it is scaring hell out of the people. We now have an unemployment rate two points higher and the Prime Minister is saying that the worst times can be the best. That is the word from the Prime Minister of Canada to the working people of Glace Bay and of the Strait of Canso, that the worst times can be the best. We want more than words of that kind from the Prime Minister of Canada. The people need action, concrete proposals to meet those problems.
The Government ought to consider the suggestion made by the workers in heavy water plants, and determine whether the

December 6, 1982
Adjournment Debate
construction of reactors cannot be accomplished across Canada and elsewhere in the world. The Government must review its plans and its programs and ensure the sale of these reactors to provide for the continuation of these heavy water plants, because if it does not, not only will the workers involved come upon economic disaster, but probably the whole Island of Cape Breton will experience an economic disaster, if it is not already in that situation at present.
1 hope the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will give a little more thought and consideration to this problem than he has in the past, that he will not content himself with the indication he gave to the parliamentary committee on November 23 when he simply said he had a proposal to close the heavy water plant and unless something happened, which he did not indicate he intended to make happen, he would have to abide by the recommendation of Atomic Energy and close the heavy water plant.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED FUTURE OF NOVA SCOTIA HEAVY WATER PLANTS. (B) POLICY ON SALES TO INDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the concerns raised by the Hon. Member, 1 wish to inform him that we, on this side, do not need to take any direction from him, or his Party, about how we should be sensitive to those workers in Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury. I should point out to the Hon. Member that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), as well as the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), met with the unions involved at both Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury and explained the situation to them. The problem we have to focus our attention on is twofold, both domestic and international. There are no foreseeable sales for Candu reactors within Canada or, indeed, on the international market.
What is more appalling. Mr. Speaker, is the hypocrisy of the Conservative Party of Canada. We have the Conservative Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), a "Crosby", unlike his colleague, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), or his colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver
Quadra (Mr. Clarke), or his colleague, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), who each want those two heavy water plants closed.
Of course, the New Democratic Party is no better, including the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). The NDP Convention of 1980 passed a resolution which in effect said, "close both those heavy water plants." Therefore, I find it somewhat despicable that the Hon. Member would come to this Chamber and put forward the case, if you will, that somehow he is concerned about the workers in those areas. It does not add up. On the one hand you have the Conservative Party arguing that the plants ought to be closed. On the other hand you have a member from Halifax, who is probably a leadership candidate provincially, trying to say to the workers in that area that he is very concerned about them.
I assure the Hon. Member that everything possible is being done to maintain the existence of the two heavy water plants in Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury, both internationally and domestically. But he ought to know and appreciate that we are in a worldwide economic recession and individuals are not buying the Candu reactor. Therefore, I suggest very politely and respectfully that the Hon. Member's hypocrisy is second to none, other than that, of course, of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and those three Conservative Members who have said time and time again that the heavy water plants ought to close. We don't need that kind of debate in the House of Commons by the Hon. Member from Halifax. Thank you.
